title: Toward a Practitioner Epistemology: A Methodological Position for Curated Depth in Fractional Professional Practice

detail.title: Toward a Practitioner Epistemology: A Methodological Position for Curated Depth in Fractional Professional Practice
detail.abstract:
Fractional practitioners are hired for what they know. They are retained and renewed for the value they deliver. A fractional CISO enters an organization to address a cybersecurity crisis; what earns renewal is the discovery that the same decisions keep stalling at the leadership level, week after week, for reasons no one in the room can name. A fractional CFO is brought in to restructure the books; what makes the engagement indispensable is the recognition that no one in the organization has the authority or the trust to surface financial reality. The subject matter expertise is the entry ticket. The interpretive work---reading the organizational system, surfacing the evergreen patterns of avoidance and defense that produced the crisis or exposed the gap---is where the practitioner's outsized value lives. And the practitioner who can do this work systematically---who accumulates a documented corpus of observations, patterns, and outcomes within each engagement---builds something more than a reputation. They build a track record that validates the cycle: client reviews that document value the organization could not have surfaced on its own, referrals that carry the practitioner's reputation into new engagements, and renewal rates that prove the work was not finished when the crisis was resolved or the gap filled. That track record---reviews, referrals, renewals---is the practitioner's evidence that structured interpretive work produces results, and it justifies a consultative premium that volume-based practice never can. The practitioner without this methodology starts from scratch every session---same expertise, no accumulation, no documented pattern recognition, no compounding proof of what the interpretive work produces. Yet no tool available to the fractional practitioner provides a methodological framework for this interpretive work. There is no preserved context within engagements, no longitudinal accumulation across observations, no structured method for surfacing what organizations cannot see about themselves, and---most consequentially---no instrument for reading the dynamics of leadership systems under change pressure, where the deliverable depends as much on what the practitioner sees forming as on what is technically delivered.

This paper presents a methodological position for a new class of augmented professional practice. With 5.6 million high-earning independent professionals in the United States alone, the fractional executive represents a permanent and growing professional class---yet the interpretive work that drives their value has no methodological foundation. It argues that such a foundation must be built on three principles: first, that organizational complexity is irreducibly human---people and process intertwined---and that any methodology that treats organizations as purely technical systems will miss the dynamics that matter most; second, that the patterns practitioners need to surface are resistant to conventional methods of discovery---surveys, structured interviews, assessment frameworks---because they operate below the level of what organizations can see about themselves, which is why they persist even when everyone agrees something needs to change; and third, that artificial intelligence can and must compound the practitioner's own analytical judgment rather than replace it, operating within a curated framework rather than on undifferentiated general knowledge.

The Undercurrent platform is the implementation of that argument. This paper grounds these principles in specific research traditions, names the theoretical foundations that explain why organizational patterns resist examination, draws the central distinction between curated analytical depth and context-free alternatives, and proposes a blinded comparative evaluation protocol to test the framework's claims.

title: Load Balancing for Large Language Model Inference Serving: A Control and Learning Oriented Survey
affiliations: The University of Manchester - Department of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, Southeast  University, Nanjing, The University of Manchester - Department of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, The University of Manchester - Department of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, The University of Manchester - Department of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, Loughborough University and The University of Manchester - Department of Electrical and Electronic Engineering

detail.title: Load Balancing for Large Language Model Inference Serving: A Control and Learning Oriented Survey
detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely deployed as interactive neural inference services, where performance depends on how compute, memory, communication bandwidth, and persistent state are allocated under non-stationary demand. This survey studies load balancing for LLM inference serving as an intelligent scheduling and resource-allocation problem for large-scale learning systems. The analysis focuses on imbalance induced by prefill–decode phase asymmetry, key–value (KV) cache residency, heavy-tailed request variability, heterogeneous hardware, and service-level objectives (SLOs). A structured review protocol codes representative studies by imbalance source, observable signals, control knobs, assumptions, limitations, and evaluation evidence. We introduce a state– action–constraint abstraction, compare six strategy families, and synthesize evaluation practice around tail latency, time to first token (TTFT), token cadence, goodput, robustness, and energy per SLO-compliant token. Open directions are discussed for long-context and multimodal serving, decentralized deployment, green inference, and autonomous self-adaptive serving.

title: Development and Industrial Validation of an Automated Aerodynamic Cleaner for Heavy-Impurity Separation in Cotton Pneumatic Conveying Systems
affiliations: Karshi State Technical university, Namangan State Technical University, Namangan State Technical University, Namangan State Technical University, Research Institute of Fiber Crops, Lukoil Uzbekistan Operating Company LLC, Jizzakh Polytechnical Institute, Urgench State University, Fergana State Technical University and Termez State University

detail.title: Development and Industrial Validation of an Automated Aerodynamic Cleaner for Heavy-Impurity Separation in Cotton Pneumatic Conveying Systems
detail.abstract:
Heavy impurities such as stones, metallic fragments, and compacted mineral clods entrained in pneumatic cotton-conveying systems can damage gin saws, increase fire hazards, disrupt processing stability, and reduce fiber quality. Conventional stone catchers often rely on manual impurity discharge, resulting in airflow disturbances, re-entrainment of impurities, and increased operational downtime. This study presents the development and industrial validation of an automated aerodynamic cleaner designed for continuous heavy-impurity removal from seed cotton without interrupting pneumatic conveying conditions.
The developed cleaner integrates three functional components within a single working chamber: an adjustable inclined grate-guide for cotton fluffing and impurity release, a front-wall grate preventing cotton loss into the collector, and a rotating drum-shaped valve enabling automated impurity discharge while maintaining negative-pressure stability. Airflow behaviour and particle trajectories were analysed using numerical modelling and SolidWorks CFD simulations. A 2³ full-factorial experimental design was applied to optimize the principal geometric parameters of the cleaner. The optimal configuration was identified as a grate inclination angle of 30°, spike spacing of 30 mm, and guide distance of 140 mm, with regression models demonstrating high predictive capability (R² > 0.96).
Laboratory investigations showed a mean heavy-impurity separation efficiency of 87%, compared with 79% for the conventional 2CHTL stone catcher. Separation efficiency for coarse impurities exceeded 98%, reaching 98–100% for particles larger than 35 mm. HVI 900-SA fiber testing confirmed that the cleaning process improved fiber strength from 42.5 to 43.1 gs tex⁻¹ and elongation from 7.0% to 7.5%, while preserving micronaire, fiber length, uniformity, and color characteristics.
Full-scale industrial trials conducted in a commercial cotton gin demonstrated 98% impurity separation efficiency, a 62.5% reduction in installed power demand, improved fiber classification grade, stable continuous operation, and elimination of fire incidents associated with heavy-impurity ingress. The developed cleaner provides a practical engineering solution for automated impurity removal in cotton pneumatic conveying systems while simultaneously improving process reliability, energy efficiency, operational safety, and fiber quality

title: Can Daoism Drive Innovation? Quanzhen, Zhengyi, and Corporate Innovation in Contemporary China
affiliations: and University Putra Malaysia - Institute for Mathematical Research

detail.title: Can Daoism Drive Innovation? Quanzhen, Zhengyi, and Corporate Innovation in Contemporary China
detail.abstract: This study examines whether sectarian differences within Daoism (between the Quanzhen and Zhengyi traditions) have left a measurable imprint on corporate innovation in contemporary China. Using geo-coded data on registered Daoist temples and firm-level research and development (R&D) data on Chinese listed companies, we find that stronger local Quanzhen presence, relative to Zhengyi, is associated with substantially higher corporate R&D investment. After addressing endogeneity, the association holds. It is not statistically significant in coastal regions; it is most pronounced among private firms in inland provinces, where cultural norms have the greatest latitude to shape managerial decisions. The findings are consistent with Daoist cultural traditions contributing to indigenous corporate innovation in China, with associations that depend on which Daoist tradition is present and where formal institutions leave room for cultural norms to operate.

title: Substitutes or Complements? How Employee Helping Behavior is Influenced by Observability and Discretionary Compensation
affiliations: Indiana University - Kelley School of Business - Department of Accounting and Villanova University - Accountancy

detail.title: Substitutes or Complements? How Employee Helping Behavior is Influenced by Observability and Discretionary Compensation
detail.abstract: Evidence suggests that organizational performance is improved when employees provide greater effort toward helping teammates. However, helping behavior is not frequently contracted upon in practice, and relatively little is known about how common elements of the control environment fundamentally influence employees’ inclinations to help others. In an experiment, we predict and find that as compared to a baseline condition where helping is not observable by the team manager and the manager has no control over employees’ compensation, employees choose greater helping behavior when either helping is observable by the manager or when the manager controls a discretionary bonus pool. We further find that the two factors interact with each other in a way that is partly substitutive, and that the separate effect of observability is greater than the separate effect of discretionary compensation. Additional results suggest that employees devote less costly (productive) effort toward helping at a greater rate than more costly (productive) effort, suggesting that the opportunity cost of effort may further play a role in helping decisions. Our study contributes to research and practice by highlighting to managers how elements of the performance information environment and common incentive contracts generate potential benefits for helping behavior that can improve individual and group outcomes.

title: CDN/TLS Termination Path Dependency as a Quantum-Vulnerable Architecture: An Outside-In Diagnosis for Regulated Banking

detail.title: CDN/TLS Termination Path Dependency as a Quantum-Vulnerable Architecture: An Outside-In Diagnosis for Regulated Banking

declarations.ethicsApproval: The author attests that the nature of this research has not, to date, required any collection of personal or private institutional data, but has nevertheless been conducted in accordance with appropriate ethical standards for research based on published sources.
declarations.funderStatement: The author did not receive any funding for this research from any source.

detail.abstract: Regulated banks increasingly terminate customer-facing transport-layer encryption not at their own infrastructure but at a third-party content delivery network (CDN) edge, where the protecting cipher is undone, customer content is processed as cleartext and the CDN applies its own fresh onward encryption. Such an arrangement leaves the bank carrying non-delegable regulatory responsibility for the confidentiality and integrity of data whose cryptography it no longer controls, can no longer observe and can no longer unilaterally change. This note argues that the arrangement is a present-tense surrender of cryptographic control and, read against the transition to post-quantum cryptography, a quantum-vulnerable path dependency that the regulated entity cannot remediate on its own terms. The argument does not depend on the timing of a cryptographically relevant quantum computer. The security literature has established that interposed TLS termination weakens connection security, but has approached the edge from two directions that miss this reading: measurement studies framed interception as something done to an organisation's own outbound traffic, using the CDN as their observation point rather than their subject; by contrast, cryptographic-protocol analyses of inbound edge termination asked only whether the cryptography was sound. Neither asked what it means to hold organisational responsibility for a cryptographic termination junction one does not control. Drawing on the scholarship on jurisdiction over data, the note shows that at the cleartext edge the authority able to compel production follows control of the terminating entity rather than the residency of the data. Thus a bank may be required to answer to its own supervisor for traffic exposed under a foreign legal order. This note locates the resulting mismatch between responsibility and control as a structural barrier to post-quantum migration, distinct from and prior to the economic barriers recent literature has catalogued, since an organisation cannot migrate, audit or reliably inventory cryptography it does not hold; and it observes that hybrid post-quantum key agreement now deployed at the edge, real as it is, protects the journey to the termination point without returning control of it. The note proposes an outside-in orientation for cryptographic readiness that takes the locus of cryptographic control, not the cryptographic asset per se, as its analytic primitive, so surfacing the structural mismatch which an inventory-first PQC migration orientation assumes away. The analysis is confined to banking regulated within the European Union, rests on public documentation and is diagnostic: architectural responses, repatriation of termination included, are treated as a decision space rather than recommended. It is offered as a programme note, framing the problem and the research agenda (in monitoring, legal duty, formal attack-surface modelling and supplier disclosure) that this problem framing logically requires.

title: Beyond Public and Private Service Commoning Service and the Reproductive Meaning of Work

detail.title: Beyond Public and Private Service Commoning Service and the Reproductive Meaning of Work

declarations.ethicsApproval: I have used artificial intelligence to find sources, parse the text, and finalize it.

detail.abstract:
Modern societies are commonly described as service societies, yet the concept of service remains theoretically unsettled. In markets, service is usually understood as a transaction between provider and customer; in public administration, as a provision, entitlement, or performance; and in platform capitalism, as a data-mediated and often invisible relation distributed across global infrastructures. These frameworks obscure the reproductive meaning of service work: the maintenance, repair, and development of the conditions under which human beings, communities, institutions, and ecosystems continue to live. 

This article develops a conceptual reinterpretation of service work through the category of the common. It reconstructs a brief conceptual history of service, from servitium and duty to utility, the service sector, the service economy, and platform service. It then revisits the legal-historical distinction between private, public, and common things, arguing that the public/private binary is insufficient for understanding the life-conditions sustained by service work. The article further argues that commoning service requires a transformation in the concept of property: from dominium, ownership as command, exclusion, and disposal, toward custodium, stewardship as responsibility for the conditions of life. Finally, it proposes the concepts of reproductive service and commoning service as ways to understand service work as civic participation in the responsible reproduction of shared life. 

The argument concludes that the service society should be reinterpreted as a reproductive society. Under ecological realism, all work-including primary production, industrial labour, technological development, care, education, administration, maintenance, repair, and cultural work-must be judged by the life-conditions it serves. Service work is therefore not a residual category of post-industrial capitalism, but one of the institutional cores of ecological civilization. To clarify how work becomes formative rather than merely necessary, the article finally draws on the Finnish concept of sivistys and reinterprets the classical fields of scholē, polis, oikos, and agora as four questions that must be returned to all work.

title: Selecting seasonal filters in X–13–ARIMA via cross-validation
affiliations: Deutsche Bundesbank

detail.title: Selecting seasonal filters in X–13–ARIMA via cross-validation

publicationDetails.journalName: Deutsche Bundesbank Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: Official statistics routinely employs the X–13–ARIMA method to seasonally adjust economic time series. A key step is choosing the length of the seasonal moving average. Traditionally, this choice relies on ad hoc criteria and expert judgement. We propose a cross-validation-based filter selection scheme that offers greater flexibility, including the possibility of incorporating novel filters. This approach is particularly promising for the seasonal adjustment of weekly, daily, and high-frequency time series. We demonstrate how to integrate cross-validation into the X–13–ARIMA method and discuss the advantages of various implementation options. Evaluation on monthly and quarterly time series demonstrates that this selection method performs at least as well as, and often better than, conventional selection criteria.

title: Examining the Role of Public-Private Partnerships in Enhancing Port Infrastructure Efficiency and Global Trade Connectivity
affiliations: Infervision - Institute of Advanced Research and Institute of Advanced Research

detail.title: Examining the Role of Public-Private Partnerships in Enhancing Port Infrastructure Efficiency and Global Trade Connectivity
detail.abstract: Ports have become more reliant on public-private partnerships (PPPs) in solving funding, efficiency and connectivity issues. Still, the effect of PPPs on the global port infrastructure efficiency and trade connectivity is yet to be fully matured. This study examines the role of PPP projects in the development, improvement and use of port infrastructure for the purposes of international trade. In line with the objective of this research work, we also focus to examines PPP initiatives in India, focusing on stakeholders' perspectives, participation, challenges, and recommendations for sustainable PPP model. The primary objective is to analyse the current PPP conditions, challenges, and the prospects for technology application in the sustainability port operations in Indian. Considering the objective of this research, a qualitative case study approach has been taken to execute this study. This research includes analysis of case studies as well as examines critical success factors, challenges, and policy implications focusing on different regions aiming at determining best practices for proper implementation of PPPs in India. The key findings reveal that PPP initiative in port operations has become a tool of enhancing the technology adoption and infrastructure development that enables the global trade connectivity. The PPP initiative enables us to overcome the barriers such as budgetary restrictions, legal weaknesses, and stakeholder reluctance to share the resources. The PPP Model enables stakeholders to prioritise investments in advanced technologies and infrastructure and enhance stakeholder engagement through regular communication and collaborative efforts. However, case analysis also reveal that more work should done in relation to regulatory issues and risk issues. The paper puts forth strategies for policymakers and the stakeholders to enhance the performance of PPP models in relevance to international trade and sustainable development.

title: The Reach of the World Cup Distraction Effect: Evidence from Global Trading Venues

detail.title: The Reach of the World Cup Distraction Effect: Evidence from Global Trading Venues

Algoseek had no role in the study design; in the collection, analysis, or interpretation of data; in the writing of the report; or in the decision to submit the article for publication.

detail.abstract: The FIFA World Cup is a clean, globally synchronized attention shock. Yet the markets that now carry most of the world's trading do not visibly respond to it in aggregate, and the headline evidence that they do turns out to be an artifact of how the effect is measured. Ehrmann and Jansen show that trades on a country's national exchange roughly halve when its team plays, carried by a local trader who is also the viewer. Two questions sit conflated on that mechanism: whether the global attention shock moves aggregate trading in the continuous, global, derivative venues where no team maps to the marginal trader, and whether the local effect generalizes beyond its first exchange. We separate them. Our most transferable result is that two natural ways of measuring the effect manufacture it from no underlying response: a cross-market comovement decline (−0.086, p = 0.005) that vanishes once the set of open instruments is held fixed, and an all-session cash-equity volume increase (+19%) that is extended-hours sampling. Each reproduces the prior finding from a process with no match effect, the comovement case shown general by a Monte Carlo. On one-minute data for eleven instruments across five market structures over 2018 and 2022, the aggregate channel is bounded near zero: equivalence tests reject a 30% effect in every group (declines beyond about 9% excluded in crypto spot, 6% pooled), and an injected 30–45% decline is recovered with full power, so these are genuine nulls, not weak tests. The local channel we bound rather than refute. No mapped venue we can reach shows a decline and the daily home response is bounded below about 11%; but the exact Ehrmann–Jansen object, a minute-level own-exchange trade count whose trader is the viewer, is left untested for want of free foreign intraday data. The next-day loser effect is absent at daily frequency in 20 national indices and 16 currencies. We do not overturn the distraction effect in its own setting; the contribution is the bound on the aggregate channel, the evidence that it does not travel to the venues that now carry most trading, and the two mechanisms that show how readily it is mismeasured.

detail.abstract: This paper examines cross-country differences in consumer expectations about macroeconomic outcomes and mortgage borrowing conditions within a monetary union. Using harmonized microdata from the ECB Consumer Expectations Survey for eleven euro area countries, we document significant national disparities. By sequentially adding a rich set of consumer- and country-specific macro controls to pooled regressions with country fixed effects, we find that these factors account for much, but not all, of the cross-country heterogeneity in expectations. These remaining differences likely reflect unobserved country specific factors, highlighting the need for country-tailored monetary policy communication to effectively stabilize consumer expectations.

detail.title: Corporate Debt Composition, Access to Credit, and Monetary Policy

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Finland Research Discussion Paper No. 7/2026
publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Finland Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: In both the U.S. and the euro area, the share of market finance in aggregate corporate credit has grown over time. To study the implications of the corporate debt structure for the transmission of monetary policy, we develop a New Keynesian DSGE model in which firms differ in productivity and may finance themselves with either bonds or loans. Our setup makes the aggregate corporate debt composition and firms’ credit access endogenous and dependent on aggregate economic conditions. The model rationalizes the empirically documented substitution from bank loans to bond finance following a monetary policy con traction. Credit is squeezed for those bank-dependent firms that cannot access the bond market. A structural shift in the aggregate bond-to-loan ratio among credit-eligible firms affects financial market dynamics, but does not materially change the overall impact of monetary policy shocks on the macroeconomy. Instead, in an economy with greater credit access, aggregate demand is less responsive to monetary policy shocks.

title: Atoms and Minds: On the Industrial Race Ahead of Us
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Atoms and Minds: On the Industrial Race Ahead of Us
detail.abstract: The public debate over artificial intelligence is conducted almost entirely in the vocabulary of software-benchmarks, parameters, model releases. This paper argues that the framing is mistaken. The contest for AI supremacy is an industrial contest, governed by two physical and human constraints that no algorithm can relax: electrical power and trained minds. Read through this lens, the present strategic picture is stark. China is building the inputs-approving roughly ten nuclear reactors in each of four consecutive years, holding the world's largest fleet under construction, and now producing close to half of the planet's elite AI researchers domestically. The United States is buying the inputs-constructing data centres at scale and importing talent through compensation packages that have reached, in one reported case, the better part of a billion dollars per individual: momentum that is real but rented. Europe is doing neither. A survey of the wider field-the Gulf, India, East Asia, and the Global South-finds the same logic everywhere: the serious builders couple energy to compute, and Europe appears on none of these maps. The paper develops this constraint-based account drawing on Smil, Perez, and Mazzucato; reframes the recurring "data centres consume too much water" narrative-and the live 2026 controversy over whether that narrative is foreign-financed-as a distraction variable; and closes with a normative proposal for a credible European response. The central claim is uncomfortable: the next decade of AI will be won by whoever keeps the lights on and grows the people-and on present trajectory, that is not Europe.

title: The Effect of Race, Gender and Priming on LLMs' Conviction Predictions
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley - School of Law and University of California, Berkeley - School of Law

detail.title: The Effect of Race, Gender and Priming on LLMs' Conviction Predictions
detail.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) could help overcome fundamental shortcomings in justice systems, by enhancing access to justice, supporting legal professionals, and ultimately promoting fairness and efficiency across legal frameworks. The hope that LLMs could improve judicial processes is tempered by concerns over AI fairness, with evidence of LLMs echoing biases deeply embedded in human cognition. This study audits the performance of two LLMs in the legal domain, specifically evaluating how a defendant's race and gender influence conviction predictions. It further tests models' sensitivity to implicit biases, measuring explicit versus implicit racial conditions using suggestive names, as well as the priming effect in AI, by introducing positive or negative context before the main prompt. We present findings from an experiment (N=17,324) in which we asked OpenAI's GPT-4 and 4o to predict conviction probabilities on a scale from 0% to 100%. Our overall 45 prompts were designed around a hypothetical criminal case scenario that had been used in prior studies with human judges, where we manipulated defendant attributes across a 3(gender) × 5(race) × 3(priming) experimental design. Our results demonstrate a small yet systematic influence of race and a clear priming effect in both tested models. Findings point to progressive bias, suggesting that both models may have undergone algorithmic debiasing.

detail.abstract: Water systems in the U.S. are required to provide notifications to consumers when they detect elevated levels of contaminants in drinking water. This paper provides the first examination of the effects of nitrate contamination notifications on home prices in California, an issue that has impacted more than 1.4 million residents in affected water systems across the state. Using a robust difference-indifferences and event-study framework with ZIP-code level housing data from 2000 to 2024, I find that nitrate contamination notifications are associated with statistically significant declines in home prices of approximately 5.8 percent in the years following a notification. These estimates imply economic costs amounting to $212.5 million for an average-sized water system.

detail.abstract:
Over the past few years, artificial intelligence—in particular, generative AI—and the changes brought about by this new technology have garnered priority attention from policymakers, commentators, and the mass media. Issues such as job displacement, the unauthorized use of personal information and likeness, the protection of intellectual property rights, and environmental sustainability have attracted analyses through an AI lens. What is less explored, however, is how AI will change the future development of international law. 

To provide an overview of the issues that have received attention thus far and that will continue to emerge at the intersection of AI and international law, this short essay, which was expanded from the opening remarks on the “Artificial Intelligence and the Boundaries of International Law” panel at International Law Weekend—West 2026, identifies eight issues that deserve greater policy and scholarly engagement. Together, these issues help demonstrate the need for a new research agenda for AI and international law and provide content to fill this agenda.

title: Is the AfCFTA Investment Protocol Fit for the Fifth Industrial Revolution? Defining and Protecting Digital Assets in Africa
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Is the AfCFTA Investment Protocol Fit for the Fifth Industrial Revolution? Defining and Protecting Digital Assets in Africa
detail.abstract: The AfCFTA Investment Protocol was negotiated against the backdrop of an accelerating digital transformation, where value is increasingly derived from intangible assets such as data, algorithms, and digital platforms. This paper critically assesses the Protocol's readiness to govern investment in the digital economy, a sector pivotal for Africa's development but fraught with regulatory challenges. It argues that the Protocol's relatively traditional definition of investment and its asset-based protections may be ill-equipped to address the unique characteristics of digital assets, creating significant legal uncertainty for investors and regulators alike. The paper examines three core areas of tension. First, it analyses whether cross-border data flows, cloud computing infrastructure, and artificial intelligence systems can be unequivocally classified and protected as covered investments under the Protocol. Second, it investigates the compatibility of the Protocol's provisions with the AfCFTA Digital Trade Protocol, particularly concerning data localisation measures and digital sovereignty. Third, it questions the suitability of the investor-state dispute settlement mechanism, the design of which remains subject to ongoing negotiation pursuant to Article 46 of the Protocol, for resolving complex, technology-driven disputes. By highlighting these potential regulatory gaps, the paper contends that without a forwardlooking interpretation by arbitral tribunals or subsequent explicit amendments, the Protocol risks failing to provide the legal certainty needed to attract high-value digital investment.

detail.title: The Manne Programs in Economics for Federal Judges

publicationDetails.detailsText: Case Western Reserve Law Review, Vol. 50, pp. 351–420 (1999)

detail.abstract:
For over twenty years, Henry G. Manne developed and directed educational programs in economics for federal judges. After starting the programs at the University of Miami Law & Economics Center (LEC) in 1976, Manne moved the LEC and its programs to Emory University in 1980 and then to George Mason University School of Law (GMUSL) when he became Dean in 1986. Over the years, the Manne Programs earned a reputation as demanding, intellectually stimulating, practical, and enjoyable experiences. Because of Manne's personal commitment, attention to detail, and warm hospitality, the programs have always enjoyed a strong following among federal judges. By 1990, approximately forty percent of the sitting federal judges had completed Manne's flagship program—the Economics Institute for Federal Judges.

The Manne Programs have influenced the thinking of a generation of federal judges. Manne, ever mindful of the potential for politically motivated attacks on his programs, was always careful to stress that the Institute focused on positive economics. He argued that there was little disagreement among economists about the theory and the logic of microeconomics, and he encouraged the judges to view economics as a practical set of tools for understanding cases. In general, the programs focused on price theory and applications to everything except legal issues. Initially, the only exception to this was the session on “Monopoly,” which necessarily included a discussion of antitrust law. Later, a session on "Law and Economics" was added in response to the judges’ desire to see how the materials were being taught in law schools. Manne intentionally left it to the judges to figure out the legal implications of the analysis. Nevertheless, it is no secret that a natural repercussion of the application of economic reasoning to legal problems is a greater appreciation of the roles of private property rights, freedom of contract, entrepreneurship, and the rule of law in a free society. Many of the judges attending the Manne Programs arrived skeptical of the alleged conservative bias of the programs, and left impressed with the analytical rigor and consistency of the economic approach to human behavior.

In terms of its popularity among judges, the success of the Manne Programs must be attributed to the high standards—both in academic substance and programmatic style—set by Henry Manne. The Manne Programs continue to be operated by the LEC at GMUSL. The real challenge for GMUSL will be to provide the energy, enthusiasm, commitment, and knowledge that are necessary to engender the same loyal following of the judges that Henry Manne enjoyed.

detail.title: Impact Washing in Venture Capital and Private Equity
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether impact-related disclosures by venture capital and private equity fund managers predict measurable portfolio impact outcomes. Using a sample of 583 European venture capital and private equity funds, we combine fund-level net impact scores from the Upright Platform with a novel Large Language Model (LLM)-based disclosure measure. Exploiting the implementation of European Securities and Markets Authority's (ESMA) naming rules, we document a weak but positive relationship between disclosure intensity and realized portfolio impact. However, the ESMA guidelines do not significantly strengthen the alignment between public impact claims and actual outcomes relative to a non-EU control group. We further find that venture capital funds exhibit higher portfolio impact scores than the rest of private equity, consistent with greater exposure to innovation-and technology-driven sectors, although these differences are not statistically significant. Overall, the findings suggest that disclosure-based regulation alone may have limited effectiveness in reducing impact washing in private markets. The paper also contributes to the emerging literature on sustainable venture capital by introducing an LLM-based framework for measuring impact disclosure quality at scale.

title: New Challenges and Opportunities in Financing Development of Asian Fragile Contexts

detail.title: New Challenges and Opportunities in Financing Development of Asian Fragile Contexts
detail.abstract: This paper examines development finance in seven fragile contexts in Asia: Afghanistan, Yemen, Syria, Iraq, Myanmar, Pakistan, and the DPRK. The paper uses the OECD concept of fragility as a multidimensional phenomenon in which exposure to risk is combined with limited capacity of the state or communities to prevent or mitigate these risks. The empirical discussion is based on the OECD States of Fragility framework, OECD CRS disbursement data for 2016-2023, AidData estimates of Chinese official finance, and publicly available data on development finance of other "new donors". The main argument of the paper is that the contexts of fragility differ a lot in Asia and there is a growing polarization among the key Asian recipients of development aid whereas some of them are increasingly marginalized by donors. In 2023 the seven cases received about USD 27.2 billion in official development assistance, but the distribution was highly uneven, with Syria and Pakistan accounting for almost 60 percent of the total. At the same time, several contexts either received very limited support or lost access to aid for political reasons. "New donors" still can not replace the OECD DAC systems as their mostly focus on strategically important or relatively stable contexts. In extremely fragile contexts, grants and humanitarian assistance remain central, while loans, guarantees, blended finance, and infrastructure projects are constrained by debt, sanctions, lack of international recognition, and weak state capacity.

title: The Double Burden of Child Malnutrition: Prevalence and Determinants of Stunting, Wasting, and Overweight in 194 Countries – An Assessment of Global Health Targets

detail.title: The Double Burden of Child Malnutrition: Prevalence and Determinants of Stunting, Wasting, and Overweight in 194 Countries – An Assessment of Global Health Targets

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is based on secondary analysis of aggregated, publicly available data and does not involve human subjects. All data were anonymized and aggregated before public release. No ethical approval was required.

detail.abstract:
Background: We evaluated global, regional, and national trends in stunting, wasting, and overweight among children under five years from 2000 to 2024 across 194 countries, assessed progress toward Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) Target 2.2, and identified key socioeconomic and spatial determinants of malnutrition.

Methods: We analysed JME 2025 data across 194 countries (2000–2024) using advanced econometric approaches including panel data models with country and time fixed effects (4,850 observations for stunting and overweight; 2,960 for wasting), spatial econometric models (spatial autoregressive and spatial error models with inverse distance weighting), quantile regression at the 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles, Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition, and Bayesian hierarchical modelling with Markov Chain Monte Carlo simulation (four chains, 10,000 iterations). Covariates included GDP per capita (PPP-adjusted), maternal education (mean years of schooling), urbanization rate, poverty headcount ratio, under-five mortality rate, access to improved water and sanitation, women's employment, food production index, conflict intensity (0–10 scale), health expenditure, and nutrition policy index (0–100).

Findings: From 2012 to 2024, global stunting prevalence declined from 26·4% to 23·2% (150·2 million children; 95% CI 146·4–154·0), wasting from 7·4% to 6·6% (42·8 million; 95% CI 34·6–52·6), including 12·2 million with severe wasting, while overweight remained unchanged at 5·5% (35·5 million; 95% CI 31·7–39·7). Africa was the only region with an increase in stunted children (+3·1 million, +5·0%). Only 14·4% of countries are on track for wasting targets and 9·3% for overweight targets, with 33·0% of countries lacking sufficient wasting data for assessment. GDP per capita elasticity was −3·842 (p<0·001) for stunting, −1·028 (p<0·001) for wasting, and +0·845 (p<0·001) for overweight. Significant spatial autocorrelation was observed for all indicators (SAR ρ=0·428, 0·316, and 0·248 respectively; all p<0·05). Maternal education (−1·826, p<0·001) and poverty reduction (0·384, p<0·001) were strongly associated with stunting. Conflict intensity (0·284, p<0·05) significantly predicted wasting. Under current trends, global stunting is projected to reach 22·8% by 2030 (95% CI 21·2–24·4), substantially above the SDG target of 13·2%.

Interpretation: Current progress on child malnutrition is insufficient to achieve SDG 2·2 by 2030. The persistent burden of undernutrition in Africa and Asia, combined with rising overweight prevalence globally—affecting 35·5 million children—represents an emerging double burden of malnutrition. Accelerated investments in maternal education, economic development, poverty reduction, and nutrition-sensitive interventions are urgently needed, alongside strengthened surveillance systems to address critical data gaps affecting one-third of countries for wasting monitoring. Without substantial acceleration in policy efforts and resource allocation, the ambition of ending all forms of child malnutrition by 2030 is unlikely to be realized.

title: Central Asia under Fragmented Globalization: Political Transition, Reforms, and the Limits of Economic Openness

detail.title: Central Asia under Fragmented Globalization: Political Transition, Reforms, and the Limits of Economic Openness
detail.abstract: This paper examines how Central Asian economies adapt to the fragmentation of globalization after 2022. The argument is not that the region has entered a new phase of political liberalization or straightforward economic opening. The more specific issue is how Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, and Turkmenistan are changing their external economic position in an environment shaped by Western sanctions against Russia, trade conflicts, bloc-based integration, and weaker global momentum for liberalization. The paper uses World Bank WDI data on GDP growth and trade openness, OECD and EBRD materials on trade facilitation and transport corridors, IMF country materials, and estimates of sanctions-related trade diversion. After 2022, growth accelerated in several countries, especially Kyrgyzstan and Kazakhstan, while Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, and Turkmenistan preserved high growth rates. Trade intensity also changed, with Kyrgyzstan's trade-to-GDP ratio rising from about 100 percent in 2021 to 132 percent in 2023. These shifts, however, are not evidence of a completed liberal transformation. They reflect new transit, re-export, logistics, payment, capital-relocation, and infrastructure functions. Reforms affect the capacity to use these channels, but they remain selective and state-coordinated. The main long-term question is whether these quasi-rents can be transformed into productivity, diversification, and durable transport routes, rather than only servicing the disruption of previous supply chains.

title:

 Singapore's Global Trader Programme and Commodity Profit Shifting in ASEAN

detail.title:
Regulatory Assymmetry by Design?
 Singapore's Global Trader Programme and Commodity Profit Shifting in ASEAN
detail.abstract: Singapore, a city-state with no natural resources, hosts over 400 international commodity trading companies and handles close to 20 per cent of the world's energy and metals trade, generating an estimated 17 per cent of its gross domestic product from the wholesale trade sector. This paper examines whether Singapore's Global Trader Programme (GTP)-a fiscal incentive offering concessionary tax rates of 5 to 15 per cent on qualifying commodity trading income-may function as a structural attractor of profit shifted from resource-owning ASEAN economies, principally Malaysia and Indonesia. Drawing on Global Financial Integrity (2026) trade misinvoicing data, OECD Country-by-Country Reporting statistics, Indonesia's 2026 government investigations into crude palm oil transfer pricing, and the empirical model of Susanti and Firmansyah (2018), the paper argues that Malaysia's cumulative trade value gap of USD 871.8 billion and Indonesia's USD 550.2 billion over 2013-2022 are consistent with-though not proven to be caused bycommodity profit routing through Singapore-based affiliated trading entities. The paper introduces the concept of "regulatory asymmetry by design" to describe a condition in which Singapore's enforcement architecture protects its own tax base without imposing any reciprocal obligation to protect sourcecountry tax revenues. Alternative explanations and methodological limitations are discussed. Policy implications for source countries, Singapore, and the ASEAN bloc are proposed.

detail.abstract: A simple puzzle motivates this paper. Turkey ranks 27th globally in digital government while scoring 31 on the Corruption Perceptions Index-placing it alongside Senegal and Bolivia. Kazakhstan ranks 24th in e-government while scoring 38 on CPI. Brazil is in the global top 50 for digital public services while its CPI suggests institutional quality comparable to Morocco. Azerbaijan (EGDI rank 74, CPI 30) has processed over 90 million public service transactions through its ASAN network and received the UN Public Service Award, yet its CPI places it alongside Sierra Leone and Djibouti. This paper asks whether these two governance indicators measure the same thing. They do not. reducing petty corruption. Project-level analysis of 43,029 OECD CRS governance records (2019-2022) reveals that within-country increases in EGDI predict a higher administrative-type aid share in subsequent years (β = +125.6, p = 0.010; N = 144 country-years; country fixed effects). The World Bank IBRD allocates 98.0% of its HCLA governance portfolio to administrative-type categories ($9.0B); only the United States systematically directs governance aid toward accountability-type programmes for HCLA states (9.8% vs 39.6%). We propose a four-dimension Governance Disaggregation Framework to align reform design with binding governance constraints.

title: Resonant Dynamics of Sovereign Debt: Productive Capacity as the Structural Signal
affiliations: Vers3Dynamics

detail.title: Resonant Dynamics of Sovereign Debt: Productive Capacity as the Structural Signal
detail.abstract: CBO's February 2026 baseline projects federal debt held by the public rising from 101 percent of GDP in 2026 to 120 percent by 2036, while net interest costs increase from 3.2 percent of GDP in 2025 to 4.6 percent by 2036. Those projections do not imply an imminent sovereign crisis. Still, they reflect a persistent deterioration in the interest-growth differential and a rising probability that the fiscal trajectory becomes a material financial-stability concern. This paper examines three structural drivers that compound that trajectory beyond what conventional budget analysis captures: reserve currency costs, security expenditure asymmetries, and deindustrialization. It then develops a productive-capacity framework as a complement to fiscal consolidation, arguing that durable debt stabilization requires both credible primary-balance adjustment and policies that sustain trend growth strong enough to keep the interest-growth differential manageable. Drawing on Federal Reserve speeches by Bernanke and Yellen, the 2025 Financial Stability Report, BIS commentary on sovereign-debt risk, and IMF work on interest-growth differentials, the paper maps the supervisory implications of elevated sovereign debt into specific transmission channels: valuation risk in securities portfolios, wholesale funding pressure, policy-space compression, and Treasury-market functioning. The central conclusion is that fiscal consolidation and productive-capacity investment are complements rather than substitutes, and that treating them as such is a prudential rather than ideological position.

title: Multi-scale neuralized Markov random field framework for ECG arrhythmia recognition

detail.title: Multi-scale neuralized Markov random field framework for ECG arrhythmia recognition
detail.abstract: Cardiac arrhythmias including premature atrial contraction, premature ventricular contraction and atrial fibrillation are major causes of global mortality but are often asymptomatic, making detection challenging with conventional short-term electrocardiogram (ECG) monitoring. While deep learning models have advanced automated ECG analysis, the existing approaches often struggle to effectively capture the multi-scale characteristics of ECG and lack mechanisms to ensure the physiological plausibility of predictions. To address these limitations, we proposed a multi-scale neuralized Markov random field (MSMRF) framework for several arrhythmias recognition. This framework explicitly formulates cardiac beat evolution as a probabilistic process and employs a multi-scale mixture model to simultaneously capture beat-level morphological features and rhythm-level patterns. We enhance a conditional variational autoencoder with information bottleneck regularization and integrate physiological constraints including dynamic time warping for morphology alignment and heart rate variability consistency loss during training to ensure clinically plausible recognitions. Experiments across two public ECG databases demonstrate that MSMRF outperforms several baselines across most arrhythmia categories. Mathematical convergence analysis and visualization further provide theoretical stability and interpretability. Future efforts will focus on multi-center validation, efficiency optimization and adaptive parameter selection for reliable real-world MSMRF deployment.

title: SAQM-MedFuse: Safety-aware Quality-driven Multimodal Fusion for Cuffless Blood Pressure Estimation and Risk Stratification
affiliations: Central South University, Central South University and Central South University

detail.title: SAQM-MedFuse: Safety-aware Quality-driven Multimodal Fusion for Cuffless Blood Pressure Estimation and Risk Stratification
detail.abstract: Background and Objective: Reliable cuffless blood pressure (BP) estimation from wearable physiological signals remains challenging under inter-subject variability, signal corruption, missing modalities, and high-BP underestimation. This study presents SAQM-MedFuse, a safety-aware quality-driven multimodal framework for joint systolic/diastolic BP estimation and BP risk stratification from synchronized photoplethysmography and electrocardiography. Methods: SAQM-MedFuse integrates modality-specific signal-quality estimation, sparse quality-conditioned expert fusion, uncertainty-aware branch credibility aggregation, anchor-guided decision refinement, safety-oriented upper-tail correction, subject-adaptive affine personalization, and split conformal reliability analysis. The model was evaluated on the public MIMIC-BP benchmark under a subject-disjoint few-shot personalized protocol, with all predictive metrics computed on the independent test-query subset. Results: SAQM-MedFuse achieved a mean absolute error averaged over SBP and DBP of 5.69 mmHg, with SBP/DBP MAEs of 7.15/4.23 mmHg. It also obtained 82.13% risk-stratification accuracy and 73.45% macro-F1, reducing mean BP MAE by at least 8.10 mmHg and improving macro-F1 by at least 38.5 percentage points relative to representative neural baselines retrained under the same protocol. Conclusions: The results indicate that safety-aware quality-driven multimodal fusion is a promising research direction for reliability-sensitive cuffless BP estimation, although the present system should be interpreted as a research-stage decision-support framework rather than a stand-alone clinical measurement device. Code, reproducibility scripts, and aggregate paper-level results are available at https://github.com/yazyeah/SAQM-MedFuse.

title: How Monetary Policy Shapes FinTech Lending: Complement or Substitute?
affiliations: The University of Sydney Business School and

detail.title: How Monetary Policy Shapes FinTech Lending: Complement or Substitute?
detail.abstract: We examine how monetary policy regimes shape fintech lending using loan-level data from Prosper Marketplace. We show that fintech lending behavior varies systematically across monetary environments and borrower types. During monetary easing, fintech lending complemented traditional banks by offering favorable terms to attract first-time borrowers and larger loans to repeat borrowers. Conversely, tighter monetary policies and heightened risks pushed fintech lenders to substitute for banks, extending credit to lower-quality borrowers with higher risk, especially in highly concentrated banking markets. These findings highlight fintech lenders’ dual role as both complements and substitutes in response to shifts in the monetary policy environment. Overall, our results provide new evidence on the regime-dependent role of fintech in credit markets and its interaction with borrower heterogeneity and banking structure.

title: The New Legal Tender Debate: Surveying State-Level Attempts to Regulate Central Bank Digital Currencies

detail.title: The New Legal Tender Debate: Surveying State-Level Attempts to Regulate Central Bank Digital Currencies
detail.abstract:
This Note explores the growing wave of state-level legislation aimed at regulating Central Bank Digital Currencies (CBDCs). CBDCs, digital forms of central bank-issued money, have sparked intense political debates between proponents who see them as the logical next development in monetary technology and critics who perceive them as threats to privacy and financial system stability. Although a widely available CBDC appears unlikely without Congressional authorization, sixteen states have enacted laws designed to preempt its development, with more statutes likely to follow. These state statutes employ various legal mechanisms, including redefining terms in the Uniform Commercial Code, prohibiting CBDC-related payments to the state, banning participation in CBDC experimentation, and excluding CBDCs as legal tender.

While acknowledging the legitimate concerns raised by CBDC skeptics, this Note argues that the enacted state statutes may create new legal risks and hinder financial innovation without effectively achieving their purported objectives. The broad language of these laws may capture a wide range of non-CBDC technologies and elements of the existing financial system, such as commercial bank reserves held at the Federal Reserve. Despite their stated goals, these laws may have unintended consequences for existing financial structures, cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin, and future innovation such as wholesale CBDCs and tokenized assets. By providing a detailed analysis of these legislative efforts and their potential ramifications, this Note calls for reassessing whether these laws serve their intended purpose. This Note finishes with recommendations for both state and federal legislators to meet their stated concerns while minimizing unintended consequences for other parts of the financial system. As global interest in CBDCs rises and domestic political pressures mount, policymakers must balance their concerns with the potential benefits and risks of these novel laws.

title: How School Choice Is Changing America's Theory of Educational Justice: From the Great Equalizer to the Great Exit

detail.title: How School Choice Is Changing America's Theory of Educational Justice: From the Great Equalizer to the Great Exit
detail.abstract: This article examines how the expansion of school choice may be reshaping America's underlying theory of educational justice. Historically, educational justice was grounded in the belief that public institutions should be strengthened and expanded to serve all children. Increasingly, however, educational reform has emphasized mobility, parental choice, and access to alternatives when public institutions fail. Drawing upon educational policy scholarship, civil rights literature, public finance research, systems theory, and emerging work in Educational Architecture, this conceptual policy analysis explores the implications of this shift. The paper argues that contemporary school choice debates reflect a broader transformation in which educational justice is increasingly pursued through individual mobility rather than institutional improvement. Through examination of the civil rights, capacity, public finance, and community transformation dimensions of school choice, the article proposes Educational Architecture as a systems-based framework for understanding educational justice beyond questions of school assignment alone. The paper concludes that while educational mobility may expand opportunities for some students, lasting educational justice ultimately depends upon the creation of stable systems, supportive conditions, and strong institutions capable of serving entire communities.

detail.title: Bayesian Non-Persuasion

publicationDetails.detailsText: Rotman School of Management Working Paper (forthcoming)
publicationDetails.journalName: University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Rules against persuasion often focus on beliefs: an institution should not manipulate the information on which a decision rests. We show that such rules can miss a distinct source of directional influence. An institution can steer an outcome without changing beliefs by selecting among authorised procedures that translate the same belief into different actions. Jury instructions provide the leading example: a judge may alter no juror's assessment of the facts yet still affect the verdict through the permissible formulation of the law. The gap is sharpest near a decision threshold. There, the scope for belief movement that preserves the default action vanishes, while procedural steering can remain maximal whenever authorised procedures disagree near the boundary, even with genuinely informative communication. In general, exposure to procedural steering is the concavification of a local steering score. The geometry of Bayesian persuasion thus reappears in reverse: it measures not the value of manipulating beliefs, but the directional discretion left open by institutional rules.

detail.abstract: Households are the fundamental unit of the American economy. Yet, despite the central role of households, recent research on consumer finance, including contributions by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), often focuses on individuals. The reason is largely practical: some of the most comprehensive sources of credit information are based on de-identified, individual-level credit records from one of the nationwide consumer reporting agencies (NCRAs). Credit record data can be an invaluable source of information for research, but they are designed to asses the risk of the individual (or individuals) listed on a credit application, not to capture the financial interactions of a household.

title: Beyond a Free Lunch: Evaluating the Trade-Offs of an Out-of-School Nutrition Program on Adolescent Girls’ Human Capital

detail.title: Beyond a Free Lunch: Evaluating the Trade-Offs of an Out-of-School Nutrition Program on Adolescent Girls’ Human Capital
detail.abstract: We study how the design of in-kind transfers can impact adolescent girls’ schooling. India’s SABLA scheme made nutrition support available outside school for girls ages 11–14. We use variation across rollout districts, birth cohorts, and gender in a difference-in-differences and triple-difference framework. The 2011 rollout increased girls’ dropout by 11% and widened the gender gap in dropout by 9%. The dropout increase is larger among girls whose mothers did not attend school and in districts where girls’ schooling was weaker before the program. A later redesign that encouraged school re-entry does not show an adverse dropout effect. Evidence on the program’s health effects suggests a 2.8% lower anemia rate among exposed cohorts measured 8–10 years after rollout. The results show a transfer-design tradeoff: support delivered outside school can protect vulnerable girls while weakening school attachment for girls near the dropout margin.

title: Introducing food co-vulnerability: Systemic exposure and selective cooperation in geopolitically fragmented regions
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and Tarbiat Modares University

detail.title: Introducing food co-vulnerability: Systemic exposure and selective cooperation in geopolitically fragmented regions
detail.abstract: Contemporary geopolitical crises have revealed the extent to which food systems are now deeply entangled with energy markets, maritime chokepoints, logistics networks and financial infrastructures. This Perspective introduces the concept of food co-vulnerability, defined as a condition in which rival or politically fragmented states remain simultaneously exposed to shared disruptions across interconnected food, energy and logistical systems. Unlike conventional understandings of interdependence, food co-vulnerability does not require political alignment, institutional integration or mutual trust. Instead, it reflects the growing systemic convergence of risks within globally interconnected food systems. Using the Persian Gulf as an illustrative case, this article argues that common exposure to disruptions in maritime trade, agricultural inputs, fertilizer markets and energy infrastructure generates forms of shared systemic risk that transcend geopolitical rivalry. At the same time, these overlapping vulnerabilities may create incentives for limited and functional forms of strategic coordination aimed at reducing collective exposure to food-system shocks. Building on debates surrounding food-system resilience, geopolitical fragmentation and weaponized interdependence, the article proposes food co-vulnerability as a conceptual lens for understanding how food insecurity may simultaneously intensify geopolitical tensions while also creating incentives for selective cooperation in an increasingly fragmented international order. The concept may also help explain emerging food-security dynamics across other import-dependent and geopolitically fragmented regions facing climate stress, strategic trade exposure and systemic supply-chain risks.

title: A Longitudinal Attribute-Conditioned Neural Network for Modeling Health-State Transition Probabilities in Temporally Irregular Data: The LANTERN Framework
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Arizona State University (ASU) - School of Mathematical and Statistical Sciences

detail.title: A Longitudinal Attribute-Conditioned Neural Network for Modeling Health-State Transition Probabilities in Temporally Irregular Data: The LANTERN Framework
detail.abstract: Accurate estimation of long-term care transition probabilities is central to disability insurance pricing, reserving, and solvency assessment. Classical actuarial multi-state models commonly rely on Markov, semi-Markov, or proportional-hazard specifications, which provide a direct connection to cohort projection but may be restrictive for irregular longitudinal health data with nonlinear aging patterns and heterogeneous covariate histories.This paper develops a well-calibrated estimator of multi-state transition probabilities for irregular longitudinal health data. The model learns from individual health history, incorporates the time elapsed between observations, and conditions transition probabilities on demographic and socioeconomic attributes. It produces a valid probability distribution over the next observed health state, with four possible states: healthy, mild disability, severe disability, and death. Individual probabilities are aggregated by age group and origin state to form transition matrices compatible with actuarial cohort projection.Using longitudinal data from the Health and Retirement Study, we compare the proposed estimator with logistic regression, gradient-boosted trees, a recurrent neural network, and a last-state persistence benchmark. The evaluation considers probabilistic accuracy, endpoint discrimination and calibration for severe disability and death, risk concentration, and transition matrix error after aggregation. The proposed estimator improves severe disability discrimination relative to logistic regression and gradient-boosted tree benchmarks, maintains strong calibration, and yields the lowest transition matrix error among the evaluated models in the held-out test analysis. These results show that a structured machine learning estimator can support long-term care transition modeling when judged by calibration and projection fidelity, beyond discrimination.

title: Unveiling Sentiment Tokens Insights for Attention-Based Transformer Models With Explainable-AI

detail.title: Unveiling Sentiment Tokens Insights for Attention-Based Transformer Models With Explainable-AI
detail.abstract: Lately, numerous companies have pivoted to use Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques to comprehend the vast amount of textual data. These include Service Requests, Customer Experience Reviews/Ratings on websites, etc. The significance of handling this data has increased substantially, as sentiment analysis and text summarization help companies derive insights and accelerate the process of resolving customer pain points. Consequently, these requirements have led to a growing demand for advanced algorithms capable of effectively handling textual data. With the Transformers introduced, the use of NLP models has increased tremendously to meet the expanding needs. However, one of the main challenges associated with Deep learning techniques is the lack of explainability, particularly for non-expert users. This research unravels the intricacies of the Transformer models and introduces a user-friendly method for calculating explainable predictions. By leveraging architectural understanding, this project aims to develop a comprehensive algorithmic framework for explaining predictions generated by attention-based models. It also intends to provide a comparative analysis of results by explaining the predictions from different Transformer models, including encoder models, decoder models, and encoder-decoder models. This paper adapts the attribution method to explain the decision-making process of various models in sequence classification tasks and then studies the comparison between the performance of different transformer models and with SHAP on Text data. Also, a novel measurement framework to validate the explanations is introduced with synonyms and antonyms of influential tokens.

title: From Stabilization to Structural Transformation: Assessing Nepal's FY 2083/84 Budget as a Policy Pivot toward a Production-Led and Digital Economy

detail.title: From Stabilization to Structural Transformation: Assessing Nepal's FY 2083/84 Budget as a Policy Pivot toward a Production-Led and Digital Economy
detail.abstract: This paper evaluates Nepal's Fiscal Year 2083/84 Budget as a strategic policy pivot from macroeconomic stabilization toward structural transformation. Departing from a consumptiondriven fiscal posture, the budget advances a reform-oriented agenda centered on production expansion, financial deepening, and digital transformation. The study develops a conceptual and empirical framework to assess whether the announced measures, spanning tax rationalization, investment facilitation, financial sector restructuring, and digital economy initiatives, can plausibly enhance growth, efficiency, and resilience. Using a mixed-method approach, the analysis combines structured policy mapping with macro-financial modeling based on Nepal's historical data on credit growth, capital formation, and digital financial adoption over the period 2005 to 2025. A reform transmission mechanism is articulated, linking fiscal incentives, financial intermediation, and digital infrastructure to productivity and growth outcomes. Empirical estimates indicate that financial deepening and digital payment expansion exhibit statistically meaningful associations with economic activity, while elevated non-performing loans exert a significant drag, implying that the budget's emphasis on fintech, credit reform, and asset resolution is directionally sound. The paper argues that the budget represents a credible shift toward a production-led and technologyenabled growth model, particularly through asset management mechanisms for distressed loans, capital market deepening, and the formalization of peer-to-peer lending. It also identifies material risks relating to implementation capacity, regulatory readiness, and institutional coordination. The study positions the budget as a policy blueprint with transformative potential, contingent upon execution discipline and governance effectiveness, and contributes to the literature by framing fiscal policy as an integrated reform instrument in emerging economies undergoing structural transition.

detail.abstract: This article proves, through three convergent arguments, that five is the optimal dimensionality of human existence. The first argument is mathematical: the volume of the unit n-ball V(n) =  n/2 / (n/2+1) is maximised at n = 5, where V(5) = 8²/15  5.264. The second is historical and economic: we trace a sphere-ball framework for Price Elasticity of Demand from the citizen-metic wealth paradox of fifth-century Athens to contemporary wealth concentration and state expansion, mapping Maslow's five-tier hierarchy onto five orthogonal longevity dimensions confirmed by Blue Zone research. The third is Bayesian: using ball-volume ratios as the likelihood function P(data | n) with a uniform prior over dimensions 1-7, the Maximum A Posteriori estimate is n = 5, robust to informative priors favouring higher dimensions. Without the sphere to define the space, the ball cannot know why its freedom decreases after five. Five is the structural constant of the relationship between self and world.

detail.abstract: Since gaining independence in 1991, Kazakhstan has made significant strides in developing its welfare state, focusing on improving life expectancy, education, and child welfare. Life expectancy, once critically low, has risen due to investments in healthcare, while education reforms have shifted from increasing access to enhancing quality through infrastructure development and vocational training. Recent policies include allocating national resource revenues to children's savings accounts, addressing child poverty, and promoting social integration. Despite progress, challenges remain in education quality, wealth inequality, and aligning government welfare delivery with public expectations. Kazakhstan's social policy evolution reflects both political necessity and developmental priorities.

title: Technological Colonization: The Rise and Demise of Elites, Nations and Civilizations

detail.title: Technological Colonization: The Rise and Demise of Elites, Nations and Civilizations
detail.abstract: A new big bang in technological development is set to unravel every bit of human and civilizational fabric starting the year 2025. 1 Many-thousand-fold more powerful new types of artificial intelligence and quantum computers, plus the fact that quantum computing powers are now in the months ahead in the hands of average consumers and citizens (this of course also refers to hackers, thieves, cheaters, and of course cartels, mafia, triads and monster-like dictators, etc.), are breaking in a new reality that takes hold of human, societal life. The perfect storm, in terms of change, is brought about by the combination of new forms of AI with new quantum computing powers, also referred to as QAI, quantum AI. This new life is devoid of slow pathways of happiness and stability, devoid of any chance for pause and poise. Thus, this new explosion of technical capabilities, powers and possibilities, is ever more so extinguishing every sniff of reality where humanity and humane passions and freedoms were prominent in the (soon-to-be) past, or the current time still, of writing this spoonful of an exposé. The technological capability explosion of the year 2025 and beyond is invading, controlling and/or crowding out, ever more life situations, ever more life moments/experiences; i.e. ever more of ever more people's life spaces and life times/moments. In short, this new big technology bang is (seemingly inexorably) extinguishing every more human freedoms with the blind promise and blind paradigm of technological 'progress' and promised-fatally supposed(!)-life 'improvements', as well as promised/supposed societal and economic 'improvements'. And these come with, and are built on (but not for, in mind or thought) ever less space and time of self-determination and privacy, human independence and hence claimed and actually lived freedoms.

title: Welfare Regime Theories: Real-Typical and Ideal-Typical Methods

detail.title: Welfare Regime Theories: Real-Typical and Ideal-Typical Methods
detail.abstract: This article provides a brief overview of different streams of welfare regime theories, which over the years, ever since the all-changing publication of Esping-Andersen in 1990, his Three Worlds of Welfare Capitalism book, have become the mainstay of comparative social policy research. The first type of welfare regime theories that prospered after the 1990 book by Esping-Andersen were real-typical welfare regime theories. Real-typical means not using Max Weber's method of ideal types. This articles also focuses on ideal type theory, especially the Ten Worlds of Welfare Capitalism Theory (or Ten Worlds Theory for short).

detail.abstract: This article provides an up-to-date discussion of the Ten Worlds of Welfare Capitalism Theory, or in short, the Ten Worlds Theory, as developed by Aspalter over the last two and a half decades. Combining the findings of mostly qualitative case study analysis (Aspalter, 2017a), plus an additional global quantitative data analysis (Aspalter, 2023a), this study discusses what the development and application of a global ideal-typical welfare regime theory means for comparative welfare state system research in general, and for the research on special cases of welfare state systems in particular. The study shown, once again, the need to distinguish ideal-typical methodology and theories, from real-typical ones. The study constitutes a part of a long-term research series developing global ideal-typical welfare regime theory, which will be an ongoing process, and which is not a means to an end, but rather the beginning of enhanced global comparative learning and a springboard for global and international welfare regime analyses of all sorts.

title: Automated Monetary Policy Sentiment Index (MPSI): A FinBERT-Driven Framework for Interpreting Central Bank Communications in the United States

detail.title: Automated Monetary Policy Sentiment Index (MPSI): A FinBERT-Driven Framework for Interpreting Central Bank Communications in the United States

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest. No personal or financial relationships with any organizations influenced this study.
