detail.abstract:
While central bank communication is a primary policy tool, quantifying the stance from qualitative FOMC text remains a significant challenge. Existing methods face a critical trade-off between the accuracy of manual coding and the scalability of machine learning. To bridge this gap, I introduce the Monetary Policy Stance Index (MPSI), a hybrid NLP framework that integrates domain-specific keywords with fine-tuned FinBERT transformers. Using an information-theoretic approach, I derive optimal weights for signal aggregation, ensuring the framework is theoretically grounded in Taylor Rule prescriptions while accurately capturing nuanced communication in FOMC meetings and Chair speeches (2020 Q1-2026 Q1). 
Validating MPSI on 168 unique Federal Reserve documents, I find that it: (i) achieves r = 0.689 (p < 0.001) correlation with the Federal Funds Rate (FFR), explaining 47.5% of FFR variance and outperforming existing text-based benchmarks by 17-67%; (ii) Granger-causes future FFR changes up to 3 months ahead (F = 8.42, p < 0.001), confirming predictive power beyond public macroeconomic data; and (iii) generates economically significant market impact, with a 10-point MPSI surprise increasing 2-year Treasury yields by 42.3 bps. Furthermore, MPSI clarity reduces term premia by 18 bps per 10-point signal strength which improves bond market functioning and lowers sovereign borrowing costs.

title: Labor Market Consequences of Generative AI: Early Evidence from Norway
affiliations: and Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU)

detail.title: Labor Market Consequences of Generative AI: Early Evidence from Norway

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Does Generative AI displace early-career workers? We provide population-wide evidence from Norwegian administrative registers, 2015 through March 2025, exploiting the November 2022 release of ChatGPT as an availability shock. Using the within-firm composition difference-in-differences employed in recent work, supplemented with a synthetic difference-in-differences at the occupation level and a firm-level shift-share design, we find no robust evidence of employment displacement among young workers in highly AI-exposed occupations, nor any robust response across other age cohorts or on incumbent labor-market outcomes. While estimated coefficients for young workers are negative, in line with the existing literature, they are small and statistically insignificant. A backdating exercise on the synthetic difference-in-differences yields larger absolute estimates than the actual treatment date across most age bands. This suggests the apparent post-2022 decline reflects, at least in part, pre-existing secular trends rather than a clean AI-period break.

title: Corrigendum: Machine Learning and Fund Characteristics Help to Select Mutual Funds with Positive Alpha
affiliations: London Business School, Universitat Pompeu Fabra, Universidad Carlos III de Madrid - Department of Statistics and CUNEF Universidad

detail.title: Corrigendum: Machine Learning and Fund Characteristics Help to Select Mutual Funds with Positive Alpha
detail.abstract: We revisit the findings of DeMiguel et al. (2023) in light of the error in the replication code identified by Fausch et al. (2025). Although correcting the error eliminates the originally reported long-only alpha, we show that the original result can be restored by refining the estimation procedure. Specifically, using a quarterly rather than annual panel, which provides a larger number of observations to train the models, employing Bayesian optimization to select hyperparameters, and rebalancing portfolios quarterly, machine learning again identifies a long-only portfolio of mutual funds with significantly positive net alpha based on the same data. We conclude that machine learning helps to select mutual funds with positive alpha, but only for investors with access to sufficiently sophisticated data and prediction models.

title: Spillovers from Global Market Connections

detail.title: Spillovers from Global Market Connections
detail.abstract: This paper studies whether global market exposure diffuses to firms that do not trade directly. Using administrative firm-to-firm transaction data, firm-level records, and customs microdata from Costa Rica, I examine initially domestic firms' first supplier relationships with globally connected domestic buyers, defined as firms that export, import, or both. Event study estimates show that suppliers experience persistent increases in revenue, corporate sales, value added, and productivity after these connections. Placebo relationships with comparable domestic buyers that are not connected to foreign markets do not generate similar gains. The effects are stronger when the new relationship represents a larger share of the supplier's sales and when the buyer has greater exposure to global sourcing markets. Connections to importer-only buyers generate more persistent gains than connections to exporter-only buyers, consistent with spillovers through foreign input knowledge, sourcing practices, and production standards. Suppliers also become more likely to export or import after the first connection and are disproportionately likely to enter the same foreign markets as their buyers. The findings suggest that domestic production networks transmit both performance gains and market-specific information, extending the gains from trade beyond firms that participate directly in international markets.

title: Regulating Platform Bias: Self-Preferencing and Transaction Fees as Strategic Substitutes
affiliations: , Michigan State University - Department of Economics, Yonsei University and Yonsei University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Regulating Platform Bias: Self-Preferencing and Transaction Fees as Strategic Substitutes

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper studies self-preferencing incentives by vertically integrated platforms that operate both marketplaces and affiliated retail businesses. We show that self-preferencing and transaction fees are substitute instruments for profit extraction, implying that restrictions on self-preferencing may induce offsetting increases in transaction fees and thereby generate unintended consequences for consumer welfare. We characterize the platform’s optimal choice of self-preferencing and transaction fees and evaluate the welfare effects of behavioral and structural remedies. We also extend the analysis to settings with platform competition and consumer search, examining how market forces shape self-preferencing incentives and evaluating the robustness of our main results.

title: Innovation without borders? The geography of technological diffusion
affiliations: European Central Bank (ECB), Harvard University - Business School (HBS), Goethe University Frankfurt, European Central Bank (ECB), University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) and European Central Bank (ECB)

detail.title: Innovation without borders? The geography of technological diffusion

publicationDetails.journalName: ECB: Working Paper Series (Topic)

detail.abstract: How well does innovation diffuse across geographic boundaries? To shed light on this question, we present a large-scale field experiment involving 3,300 firms across twelve European Union countries. We elicit firms’ perceptions of the share of similar firms in their own country that had invested in artificial intelligence (AI), as well as the corresponding share among similar firms in Germany, France, and Italy. We randomly provide half of the sample with accurate information about both domestic and foreign AI investment. We show that firms substantially underestimate competitors’ current AI investment, both domestically and abroad, and that they update their expectations about competitors’ future AI investment in response to the information treatment. The treatment also causes a statistically significant increase in firms’ own expected AI investment rate. We find strong strategic complementarities within borders: a 1 pp increase in the expected share of domestic peers investing in AI raises a firm’s own expected AI investment rate by 0.570 pp. These complementarities are absent across borders: the effect of an increase in the expected share of foreign peers investing in AI on a firm’s own expected AI investment rate is statistically insignificant. Overall, our evidence shows that innovation diffusion and strategic complementarities in AI investment are much stronger domestically than internationally.

title: Effectiveness of supervisory activities in mitigating banks’ commercial real estate risk
affiliations: ,  and European Central Bank (ECB)

detail.title: Effectiveness of supervisory activities in mitigating banks’ commercial real estate risk

publicationDetails.journalName: ECB: Working Paper Series (Topic)

detail.abstract: We assess the effectiveness of supervisory activities in mitigating credit risk stemming from banks’ commercial real estate portfolios. We analyse two activity types deployed by European banking supervisors: (a) on-site inspections, which assess in depth banks’ risk-taking and internal controls, but can only be selectively applied, and (b) off-site targeted reviews, which survey risk management practices across institutions, are less intrusive but are applied more widely. Using quarterly confidential supervisory data for large euro area banks between 2020 and 2024, we employ a Difference-in-Differences framework with an event-study design to capture the effects of these activities on the coverage ratio of banks’ commercial real estate portfolios. We find that on-site inspections are followed by persistent increases in coverage ratios, while targeted reviews are associated with immediate improvements which are significant but short-lived. The results highlight the complementary nature of the two activity types, which have different outreach possibilities and effects.

title: Innovation, Human Capital, and Taxation
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Innovation, Human Capital, and Taxation

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Canada’s innovation performance has been strong but shows limited upward momentum despitegenerous research and development (R&D) subsidies. This paper develops an endogenous innovation, multisector, heterogeneous-agent model calibrated to the Canadian economy to evaluate fiscal policies thatpromote innovation and growth. The impact of R&D subsidies depends critically on the supply of high-skilledlabor. When the supply of scientists is inelastic, subsidies raise research wages, crowd out private R&D, andcan reduce long-run growth. When labor supply is more elastic, subsidies generate substantial gains ininnovation and output. The analysis also compares alternative policy instruments. Investment tax reductionsand education spending foster innovation through capital deepening and an expanded supply of highskilledlabor, delivering more robust gains when talent constraints bind, while personal income tax changes have more limited effects. R&D subsidies also increase inequality by disproportionately benefiting high-skilled workers, although these effects are mitigated when labor supply responds. Overall, effective innovation policy requires combining R&D incentives with policies that expand human capital and reduce distortions to investment.

title: The Architecture of Irrationality: Behavioural Biases and Sentiment Dynamics in Digital Asset Markets
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Architecture of Irrationality: Behavioural Biases and Sentiment Dynamics in Digital Asset Markets
detail.abstract:
This paper develops the Integrated Digital Asset Behavioural Model (IDABM), a novel four-variable framework that formalises the joint influence of social velocity, heuristic load, platform gamma, and liquidity leverage on the price formation and stability of digital assets. The model addresses a critical gap in the literature: existing behavioural finance research treats cryptocurrency, Decentralised Finance (DeFi), and Non-Fungible Token (NFT) markets as bias-homogeneous, despite the fact that each sub-class activates structurally distinct psychological profiles.

Employing an integrative narrative review and synthesis of empirical evidence spanning 2014–2025, this study draws on peer-reviewed behavioural finance literature, on-chain analytics from Glassnode and CryptoQuant, NLP-derived social-media sentiment datasets, and case evidence from the 2022 Terra/Luna and FTX collapses. A cross-asset bias taxonomy is constructed, demonstrating that store-of-value assets (Bitcoin) are dominated by scarcity heuristics, DeFi protocols by complexity bias and yield-blindness, NFTs by affect and identity dynamics, and meme coins by concentrated FOMO-herding loops.

Three principal findings emerge. First, the absence of conventional cash-flow anchors creates a structural valuation vacuum that produces heuristic dominance in price discovery. Second, herding and FOMO are not merely present but are structurally amplified by platform gamma the gamification of trading interfaces that reduces rational friction and compresses sentiment cycles to millisecond timescales. Third, the cyclical theory of behavioural risk is empirically supported: FTX, Terra/Luna, and recurring boom-bust cycles share a common behavioural anatomy formalised by the IDABM equation: Market Stability ∝ 1 / (Sv × Hl × Pγ × Ll).

The paper concludes that effective regulation must shift from informational disclosure toward behavioural guardrails, including algorithmic accountability for social-media recommendation engines, UI/UX ethics regulation of gamified trading platforms, and behavioural literacy requirements as digital circuit-breakers. The IDABM bridges financial economics and Human–Computer Interaction (HCI), providing both researchers and regulators with a testable framework for measuring how technological environments multiply investor bias.

title: Beat the heat, the role of heat waves and droughts in regional EU economies
affiliations: , , , Banco de España, Banco de España and European Central Bank (ECB)

detail.title: Beat the heat, the role of heat waves and droughts in regional EU economies

publicationDetails.journalName: ECB: Working Paper Series (Topic)

detail.abstract: Europe is increasingly exposed to heat waves and droughts, but their short-term economic effects across sectors remain hard to predict. This study develops climate-augmented models to predict real growth in per capita value added across 1,117 EU regions (2002–2022), by combining economic indicators with high-frequency climate data. When using machine learning (ML, Random Forest and XGBoost), climate variables improve predictions in agriculture, while gains for other sectors are limited and do not outperform economic models. Heat wave indicators consistently enhance predictive performance, whereas drought effects vary by sector. Simulations of extreme combined heat and drought scenarios suggest that agricultural annual growth could fall by 1.9 to 7.6 percentage points in most regions, whereas industry, and manufacturing in particular, is less affected, although impacts are more pronounced in Eastern Europe and the Baltic states. Overall, ML models better reflect complex climate–economic interactions, supporting their use for early warning, policy planning, and targeted adaptation.

title: Biomedical Sciences as a Foundation for Kenya's Bio-Economy: From General Degrees to a Competency-Based Higher National Diploma in Natural Products
affiliations: and

detail.title: Biomedical Sciences as a Foundation for Kenya's Bio-Economy: From General Degrees to a Competency-Based Higher National Diploma in Natural Products
detail.abstract: Biomedical sciences in Kenya, including biochemistry, biotechnology, microbiology, and biostatistics, were originally positioned to solve community health needs. However, curriculum design has remained too general, theory-heavy, and hospital-centric, with no training in product development, Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP), or regulatory affairs. Graduates are unprepared for community job markets; hospital positions are saturated, and industries such as biopharma, cosmetics, and agri-biologics hire other cadres. Kenya now imports over Ksh 150 billion annually in drugs, cosmetics, nutraceuticals, and vaccines that local graduates could produce.¹² This failure persists despite demonstrated local capacity; for example, herbal formulations developed and tested by Kenyan researchers have shown efficacy in managing HIV/AIDS and COVID-19, yet these innovations have not translated into scaled commercial products due to skills and regulatory gaps. A KNQA tracer study found that only 22% of Applied Biology graduates (a related diploma program) were employed within two years.¹ Fortunately, Kenya has recently adopted Competency-Based Education and Training (CBET), established KNQF Level 7 equivalence between a Higher National Diploma (HND) and a Bachelor's degree, launched a National Dual Training Policy, and put in place a Recognition of Prior Learning (RPL) framework. This paper therefore proposes a fundamental restructuring: a KNQF Level 7 HND in Natural Products Bio-Economy, delivered under the TVET’s CBET framework. Five industrial frontiers, namely: biopharmaceuticals, bio-cosmetics, nutraceuticals, agri-biologics, and industrial microbiology, are translated into competency units, dual-training placements, and a final capstone project that produces a product dossier instead of a traditional thesis. University research partners in pharmacology and pharmacognosy provide advanced testing and articulation pathways, and the proposed cadre (Registered Biomedical Scientist – Natural Products) will be anchored within existing regulatory bodies (KMLTTB, KEMRI, PPB) rather than creating a new board. By 2030, this model aims to produce 10,000 certified practitioners, reduce relevant imports by 30%, and lower graduate unemployment to below 15%.

title: Risk-Off Already Priced In: Average Dynamics and Tail Risk in Small Open Economies

detail.title: Risk-Off Already Priced In: Average Dynamics and Tail Risk in Small Open Economies
detail.abstract: This paper examines how US financial uncertainty shocks affect portfolio investment inflows in a group of 15 small open economies (SOEs) spanning advanced markets and regionally representative emerging markets. The analysis proceeds in two complementary studies, each conditioning on the state of global risk appetite to capture asymmetric transmission. The first study, using a threshold VAR, documents that uncertainty shocks transmit significantly to financial conditions, while capital inflow responses remain muted on average and adjust more rapidly than other variables. The second study, based on panel quantile regressions, reveals that shock effects on capital inflows are concentrated at the extreme left tail of the conditional distribution, providing direct evidence of tail risk in the SOE sample. Combining the evidence from both studies, two state-dependent mechanisms emerge. In the risk-off state, characterized by depressed global risk appetite, the negative shock effect on portfolio inflows is attenuated, consistent with an already-priced-in mechanism, while equity inflows exhibit a bargain-hunting pattern where non-resident investors withdraw less from SOE equity markets, partially offsetting the negative shock effect. Both mechanisms are especially marked among SOEs with advanced and open capital markets. These findings call for policymakers in SOEs to monitor distributional indicators of capital inflow vulnerability, remain attentive to tail risks that build during risk-on periods, and prepare for rapid swings in equity inflows in the near horizon following an external uncertainty shock.

title: Roads to Commercialisation? Rural Infrastructure and Crop Portfolio Composition Among Ethiopian Smallholders: Evidence from the Ethiopia Socioeconomic Survey Panel, 2013–2016

detail.title: Roads to Commercialisation? Rural Infrastructure and Crop Portfolio Composition Among Ethiopian Smallholders: Evidence from the Ethiopia Socioeconomic Survey Panel, 2013–2016

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced this study. This research was conducted independently with no institutional or commercial affiliations.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study uses anonymised secondary survey data from the Ethiopia Socioeconomic Survey, which is publicly available through the World Bank Microdata Library. No primary data collection involving human participants was conducted. Formal ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The analysis uses publicly available data from the World Bank Living Standards Measurement Study — Integrated Surveys on Agriculture (LSMS-ISA) programme.

detail.abstract: Between 2011 and 2016, Ethiopia built more than 62,000 kilometres of rural roads under the Universal Rural Road Access Program. Did it change what farmers grew? We track 2,367 rural households across two waves of the Ethiopia Socioeconomic Survey, 2013/14 and 2015/16, and estimate the within-household change in cash crop plot share using a first-difference specification. Road distance has no statistically significant effect on crop portfolio composition over this period (β =-0.0002, t =-0.06, p = 0.953). What does predict commercialisation is household wealth: each step up the welfare distribution is associated with a 0.75 percentage point larger increase in cash crop share (β = 0.0075, t = 3.36, p = 0.001), and the richest quintile increased its cash crop share at five times the rate of the poorest. The pattern holds after controlling for elevation, rainfall, and market distance. We interpret the null result as evidence that road access reduces transport costs without addressing the risk, capital, and knowledge constraints that keep poor households anchored in subsistence production. Agricultural transformation in rural Ethiopia is less a transportation problem than it is a financial one.

title: Does GAAP Compliance Matter to Municipal Bond Investors?
affiliations: University of Chicago, Harris School of Public Policy, Center for Municipal Finance

detail.title: Does GAAP Compliance Matter to Municipal Bond Investors?
detail.abstract: Small municipalities across the United States routinely prepare financial statements on a cash-basis rather than under the generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) established by the Governmental Accounting Standards Board (GASB). In doing so they trade away visibility into their long-term financial condition for simpler, less costly reporting. Conventional wisdom holds that this information gap will narrow the pool of willing bond investors, reduce secondary market participation, and raise borrowing costs. But that claim is largely untested. Using general obligation bond issuances from Illinois municipalities from 2000 to 2024 linked to State Comptroller administrative data, I find that cash-basis issuers pay roughly three to five basis points more when they borrow, are significantly less likely to attract secondary market investors, and show declining bond market activity in the years after switching away from GAAP. A regression discontinuity at the state's 800-person threshold for mandatory professional audit confirms that financial oversight increases investor participation. These findings are directly relevant to legislative proposals in several states to relax local GAAP reporting requirements, and suggest that the bond market costs of doing so are real and recurring.

title: Analyzing Occupational Licensing Across Nations
affiliations: Stanford University and Humphrey School of Public Affairs

detail.title: Analyzing Occupational Licensing Across Nations
detail.abstract: Relatively little is known about occupational licensing across nations. Despite a large literature on occupational licensing in the United States, cross-national evidence remains scarce, especially for developing economies. We assemble harmonized estimates of licensing prevalence for 44 countries by combining new nationally representative surveys (including newly conducted nationally representative surveys for a number of previously unstudied countries) for several Latin American, African, Asian, European, and North American estimates. We document substantial cross-country dispersion in occupational licensing prevalence, ranging from roughly 14 percent of workers in Denmark to more than 40 percent in India and South Africa, the two most heavily licensed labor markets in our sample. Across countries, licensed workers generally earn higher wages than comparable unlicensed workers, with pooled Mincerian regressions implying a licensing wage premium of roughly 14 percent after controlling for worker characteristics and country fixed effects. Occupational licensing prevalence is also negatively associated with GDP per capita and governance quality, and positively associated with informal employment. While these relationships are descriptive rather than causal, they suggest that occupational licensing may be intertwined with broader institutional characteristics affecting labor market efficiency, formal-sector participation, and long-run economic development.

title: Efficient and Scalable Fine-Tune of Language Models for Genome Understanding
affiliations: New Mexico Institute of Mining and Technology, Cedars-Sinai Medical Center, University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) - Department of Statistics, New Mexico Institute of Mining and Technology and Cedars-Sinai Medical Center

detail.title: Efficient and Scalable Fine-Tune of Language Models for Genome Understanding
detail.abstract: Foundation models trained on DNA sequences have transformed genomic prediction, yet repeated adaptation across many genomics tasks remains computationally demanding and is often limited by modest labeled datasets and the narrower diversity of genomic pretraining corpora. In contrast, natural language foundation models, trained on broad textual corpora, provide transferable contextual priors and flexible conditioning mechanisms that remain underexplored in genomics. Here, we present \textsc{Lingo}: \textsc{L}anguage prefix f\textsc{In}e-tuning for \textsc{G}en\textsc{O}mes, a framework that repurposes language models for genome interpretation by embedding biological context through textual prompts and adapting model weights with adaptive rank sampling. On 17 benchmarked genomic datasets, \textsc{Lingo} achieves competitive or superior performance relative to widely used DNA foundation models while training fewer than 2\% of backbone parameters. To extend \textsc{Lingo} to longer genomic inputs, we further introduce a learned DNA sequence summarizer that aggregates token-level representations with learned landmark vectors for longer-sequence histone-mark prediction. Beyond predictive performance, we show that prompt-conditioned attention aligns with biologically active regions such as H3K27ac ChIP-seq peaks and recovers known sequence motifs. These results suggest that natural-language pretraining can be efficiently recalibrated to highlight biologically meaningful regulatory patterns, and that the observed attention-H3K27ac alignment remains detectable in an independent cell-line context, offering a scoped path toward scalable and interpretable genome modeling. Together, these results challenge a quiet assumption in the field: that genomic prediction requires genomic pretraining. We show that a natural-language backbone with the right adaptation interface reaches the same performance frontier as DNA foundation models at a fraction of the cost, and that an ablation against random initialization isolates text pretraining itself as the source of the gain. Crucially, we introduce a learned DNA sequence summarizer that replaces single-token CLS pooling with learned landmark vectors querying the encoded sequence through cross-attention; this aggregation primitive is what allows the alternative paradigm to scale, and we evaluate it at two sequence lengths. On the 1000-bp Histone (Human) benchmark, \textsc{Lingo}-trained OPT-350M reaches 86.7 AUROC at 6.2M trainable parameters, ahead of HyenaDNA (86.3, 7M) and DeepSEA (85.6, 40M). On the 8192-bp ultralong-range variant of the same benchmark, \textsc{Lingo}-trained OPT-350M reaches 90.2 AUROC at 6.5M trainable parameters, ahead of HyenaDNA (89.3, 3.5M) and BigBird (88.7, 110M); the margin over dedicated long-context DNA architectures grows as inputs lengthen, not shrinks. We argue that \textsc{Lingo} is therefore not an additional DNA foundation model but an alternative paradigm for how regulatory genomics prediction can be built and adapted, with the learned DNA sequence summarizer as the load-bearing component that makes the paradigm extend from kilobase to ultralong-range genomic contexts.

title: Examining the Hypothesis of the Influence of Family Decline on Secularization with Reference to Iranian Society
affiliations: and Institute of higher education in the Humanities

detail.title: Examining the Hypothesis of the Influence of Family Decline on Secularization with Reference to Iranian Society
detail.abstract: Introduction and Objectives: Assuming the effect of religious decline on family decline, this paper attempts to examine the contrary hypothesis: that family decline influences the decline of religion. The purpose of the article is to emphasize the need to pay more attention to the family institution in the analysis of secularization, as theorists of secularization have often neglected it. The research method is a mixed approach: a secondary analysis of empirical and historical data on the impact of family status on secularization, a content analysis of relevant statements in Islamic texts, and a comparative assessment of these results with Mary Eberstadt's theory. The study concludes that the hypothesis of family decline influencing secularization in contemporary societies is defensible based on both empirical evidence and intra-religious evidence. Thus, the consolidation of the family institution can be considered the most important, or at least one of the most important, obstacles against the trend of secularization.

title: Two-Scale Topological Momentum and Stress Regimes in Correlation Networks: Evidence from Equity Markets

detail.title: Two-Scale Topological Momentum and Stress Regimes in Correlation Networks: Evidence from Equity Markets
detail.abstract: We study synchronization transitions in financial markets via persistent homology applied to time-varying correlation networks. Vietoris--Rips filtrations on rolling Mantegna distance matrices (49 Fama--French industry portfolios, 1976--2026) capture one-dimensional homological cycles H1 that reflect intransitive sectoral triples - configurations where two pairwise correlations are strong but the third is weak. Exact analytical null distributions for the persistence and count of such intransitive precursors in random metric spaces are derived. The data reveal a two‑scale topological response: stress amplifies intransitivity among the most strongly correlated industries while dissolving it among weakly and moderately correlated ones. Because static topological summaries are highly collinear with average correlation, we assess the predictive ability of the momentum of topological reorganization for market stress onset.  At short horizons (5--20 days) the momentum of average pairwise correlation dominates, but at 60--100 day horizons the standardized rate of change of the persistence-weighted mean cycle birth  significantly outperforms both a correlation-only control and the momentum of average correlation itself. Decomposing cycles into sectoral triples maps abstract topology onto interpretable linkages. The findings show that higher-order topological momentum captures a slow, structural component of stress build-up complementary to fast-moving correlation dynamics.

detail.abstract:
Objective: This study investigates how divergent institutional environments shape the architectural design, compliance strategies, and credit outcomes of hybrid decentralizedcentralized finance platforms targeting SME working capital. Methods: Grounded in institutional logics and platform governance theory, we conduct a qualitative-dominant multiple-case analysis contrasting Poland's MiCA-aligned regulatory ecosystem with Nigeria's evolving central bank framework. Data triangulation integrates policy documents, platform technical architectures, and executive interviews across six hybrid lending models. 
Findings: Institutional asymmetry functions as a core design catalyst rather than operational friction. Mature-market platforms embed compliance-by-design protocols and tokenized liquidity routing, while emerging-market architectures rely on alternative-data underwriting and adaptive capital pooling. Cross-case synthesis reveals three hybrid typologies-regulatory adaptive, liquidity-bridged, and governance-mediated-each balancing decentralization, compliance, and capital efficiency according to local institutional constraints.
Implications: Regulators should replace rigid prohibitions with proportional sandboxes enabling iterative compliance testing. Developers must prioritize jurisdiction-aware risk modeling and interoperable middleware to scale hybrid credit without sacrificing regulatory legitimacy. 
Contribution: We advance a context-sensitive architecture framework that reframes financial reintermediation as strategic institutional alignment. By demonstrating how regulatory logics directly configure platform design, the study delivers actionable blueprints for compliant, scalable SME financing across heterogeneous markets.

title: Governing the Post-ASI Society: A Parametric Simulation Model for Policy Design in an Artificial Superintelligence Era

detail.title: Governing the Post-ASI Society: A Parametric Simulation Model for Policy Design in an Artificial Superintelligence Era

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is a computational simulation study and does not involve human participants, patient data, or personal information. Therefore, ethics approval is not applicable.

detail.abstract:
What happens to human meaning and purpose when ASI solves every economic problem? This study proposes an 18-parameter parametric equilibrium model to quantitatively simulate the social structure of a post-Artificial Superintelligence (ASI) society, with particular focus on the dimensions of human fulfillment that economic prosperity alone cannot provide.
Building upon a prior UBI fiscal simulation model (Shuichi ITO, 2026), the framework integrates six domains — technology, economy, healthcare, governance, human relationships, and demography — into three output indicators: the Ikigai Index (an original indicator quantifying meaning, purpose, and fulfillment in life), the Social Stability Index, and the Utopia/Dystopia Index.
Wide-Range Rate of Change (WRRC) sensitivity analysis reveals that the top four most influential parameters — UBI level (WRRC 65.4), inequality index (56.4), democracy level (47.6), and surveillance level (46.1) — all belong to Category A (directly controllable through policy). This provides quantitative evidence that the direction of post-ASI society is determined not by technological parameters, but by policy and institutional choices. The Ikigai Index is governed by a trinity of UBI level (68%), human labor value (71%), and human autonomy (53%), while AI labor substitution rate — despite its +85% influence on social stability — has only a +28% effect on the Ikigai Index, demonstrating the structural decoupling of economic prosperity and human fulfillment. The baseline Utopia/Dystopia Index of −75.5 at median parameter values demonstrates that dystopia is the default outcome absent deliberate policy intervention.
Two critical threshold effects are identified: an Ikigai collapse threshold when AI/robot intimacy substitution exceeds 97%, and a dystopia fixation threshold when surveillance level surpasses 50%. Comparative analysis of five archetypal scenarios — Symbiotic Utopia (+73.7), Surveillance Dystopia (−100.0), Inequality Collapse (−100.0), Meaning Collapse (+16.0), and Human-Robot Symbiotic Society (+29.6) — confirms that economic prosperity is necessary but not sufficient for human flourishing. Notably, 4 of 5 scenarios produce long-term population decline; only the Symbiotic Utopia scenario — requiring simultaneously high AI governance (90%), UBI adequacy (160%), and near-universal healthcare access (95%) — achieves population stability, suggesting that mismanagement of the post-ASI transition carries a non-trivial risk of civilizational demographic contraction.

title: Agent Experience: A Measurable Approach to Machine-Operable Environments
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Agent Experience: A Measurable Approach to Machine-Operable Environments
detail.abstract: This paper introduces Agent Experience (AX) as a measurable approach to evaluating environments for autonomous and semi-autonomous software agents. AX treats the machine-facing environment as an analytically distinct object of study, separate from human-facing interface design. User Experience (UX) measures the quality of screen-mediated human interaction; AX measures the quality of signal-mediated machine interaction. The paper defines AX as the measurable quality of an environment for software agents, operationalized through discoverability, signal clarity, executable affordances, protocol interoperability, identity verification, consent, auditability, cost attribution, and outcome verification. The approach draws on information-field theory and institutional analysis, where environments are treated as structured fields through which signals propagate and where divergence between declared rules and observed behavior can be measured as institutional anomie. AX is grounded in observable evidence from existing standards and protocols, including Agent-to-Agent (A2A) for peer-agent coordination, the Model Context Protocol (MCP) for tool and context integration, OpenAPI for service description, Schema.org Actions for web affordances, W3C Decentralized Identifiers and Verifiable Credentials for identity and claims, OpenTelemetry for traces, and NIST AI RMF for governance. The paper develops an AX measurement model, adds token-and tool-level cost modeling, maps protocol layers, compares registry implementations, and applies the approach to browser-based platforms, structured tender environments, and agent-native commerce. The contribution is theoretical, operational, and measurable: AX provides a vocabulary and method for asking how suitable an environment is for agents to complete real tasks under explicit policy, identity, cost, and consent constraints.

title: From National Quality Infrastructure to Productivity in Emerging Asia: Evidence from Vietnam
affiliations: Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation, Ministry of Science and Technology, Vietnam, CSIRO Data61, Hanoi University of Science and Technology and Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation

detail.title: From National Quality Infrastructure to Productivity in Emerging Asia: Evidence from Vietnam
detail.abstract: Quality infrastructure, comprising metrology, standardisation, conformity assessment, and accreditation, is increasingly recognised as an institutional and technical foundation for sustainable productivity growth. National Quality Infrastructure (NQI) enhances economic performance through multiple channels, including increasing market access, reducing information asymmetry, and supporting technology diffusion. However, existing empirical studies mainly focus on individual components and provide limited quantitative evidence on the macroeconomic contribution of integrated NQI systems, particularly in emerging Asian economies. This study develops the first Vietnam Quality Infrastructure Index (VQII) to measure the evolution of Vietnam’s NQI capacity over the period 2000–2023 using grounded indicators that reflect the country’s institutional context. Using a dynamic autoregressive distributed lag (ARDL) framework, the study finds a positive and statistically significant lagged relationship between VQII and total factor productivity growth. The findings suggest that the productivity effects of NQI development are gradual and become more evident after approximately three years. The results highlight the importance of long-term and coordinated investment in standards, metrology, accreditation, and conformity assessment systems as part of broader productivity enhancement and industrial upgrading strategies in emerging Asian economies.

title: More Than Just a Game? Soccer Tournaments and Firm Sentiment
affiliations: Ifo Institute and Ifo Institute

detail.title: More Than Just a Game? Soccer Tournaments and Firm Sentiment

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper provides the first systematic firm-level analysis of how major international football tournaments affect business sentiment. We combine 2.2 million responses from the ifo Business Survey with information on 17 FIFA World Cups and UEFA European Championships between 1991 and 2024 and estimate event-study models around each tournament. Our results reveal a pronounced asymmetry: firms' assessments of their current business situation barely respond to tournaments, whereas the probability of reporting better business expectations rises by around six percentage points two months before a tournament starts, remaining elevated well into the post-tournament period. The anticipation effect is strongest in manufacturing, while trade is the only sector in which the current situation also improves, consistent with tangible tournament-related demand. The European Championship, played on the continent, lifts both sentiment dimensions, whereas the World Cup operates almost exclusively through expectations. Comparing the 2006 World Cup (hosted), the 2014 World Cup (won), and the EURO2024 (hosted), we find that strong public engagement and a supportive macroeconomic environment, rather than hosting status, drive the sentiment response. A placebo test and an alternative dummy assignment based on exact survey participation dates support the interpretation that the documented effects are genuinely tied to the tournaments rather than to seasonal or cyclical patterns.

title: No Calm Before the Storm: Typhoons, Shipping, and Trade
affiliations: Musashi University, ,  and

detail.title: No Calm Before the Storm: Typhoons, Shipping, and Trade

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Extreme weather is becoming more frequent and severe worldwide, yet its consequences for global trade channels remain an open question. This paper quantifies the cost of extreme weather to maritime trade. Integrating daily typhoon wind-swath data with hundreds of thousands of vessel voyages in Japanese waters, we document that maritime traffic falls by up to roughly 50% on typhoon-exposed open-ocean cells and by about 7% at typhoon-exposed ports. A voyage-level framework identifies $119 million in direct shipping-industry costs over 2013–2021. This disruption implies a total trade-volume welfare loss of $117.8 million. Combining the two channels yields a central total welfare estimate of approximately $237 million. As climate change intensifies, the invisible costs associated with increased extreme weather will scale accordingly, highlighting a vital dimension of climate risk that remains overlooked by adaptation frameworks focused solely on catastrophic land-based destruction.

title: The First Exploratory Analysis Comparing Gender Identity with Sex assigned at Birth on Food Calorie Perception Accuracy
affiliations: University of California, Bajec Senseworks and Brown University

detail.title: The First Exploratory Analysis Comparing Gender Identity with Sex assigned at Birth on Food Calorie Perception Accuracy
detail.abstract: Food calorie estimation accuracy remains poor despite the prevalence of caloric labeling and decades of public health efforts to educate US consumers. Research on this topic comparing performance based on traditional sex differences has yielded mixed results. No study to date has examined how gender identity in comparison to sex assigned at birth (SAAB) impacts calorie perception accuracy. To explore this question, 348 individuals aged 18-23 provided their SAAB and current gender identity and estimated the calories in nine sweet and savory restaurant menu item descriptions using 100-calorie increments. Accuracy categorized by SAAB revealed minimal differences. By contrast, when the data were segmented by gender identity more heterogeneous point estimates were observed with gender-diverse participants distinguished by highest accuracy and transgender participants distinguished by lowest accuracy. Different patterns were also observed as a function of how accuracy was defined, food flavor profile (sweet v. savory) and the specific foods assessed. Gender identity reveals important and until now unknown insights into food calorie perception and brings awareness to groups at risk for unhealthy eating behavior.

detail.title: Credit Risk Externalities: Evidence from European Non-Performing Loan Spillovers

publicationDetails.detailsText: Swiss Finance Institute Research Paper No. 26-45

detail.abstract: This paper examines ex-post credit-risk externalities in Europe by quantifying crosscountry spillovers in non-performing loan (NPL) dynamics across 30 European countries over 2010Q1-2022Q2. Using a multilateral connectedness framework, we document three facts. First, spillovers are substantial: the static total connectedness index is 77.51%, indicating strong system-wide interdependence in realised credit risk. Second, NPL spillover directions are asymmetric: 18 countries are net receivers and 12 are net transmitters, where network evidence reveals a hub-and-periphery structure in which several highly connected nodes are not the economies with persistently high NPL ratios or acute domestic stress. Third, interconnectedness is persistent: dynamic rolling estimates remain elevated (typically 86-92%) and are comparatively smoother during 2019-2021, consistent with COVID-19 pandemic-era interventions dampening short-run fluctuations without dampening spillovers. Panel evidence links spillover roles to trade openness, GDP growth, and supervisory capacity: more open economies tend to be stronger net transmitters, while higher GDP growth and stronger supervisory capacity are associated with weaker net transmission.

detail.title: Do Banks Price Pollution Risk?

publicationDetails.detailsText: Swiss Finance Institute Research Paper No. 26-46
publicationDetails.journalName: Swiss Finance Institute Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper examines when and how pollution risk is priced in bank loan markets. Using toxic emission intensity as a proxy, we find that pollution risk has little effect on loan spreads in non–stress-testing periods, while conventional credit risk is strongly priced. When firms’ relationship banks are subject to regulatory stress testing, pollution risk becomes significantly priced, with spread effects comparable to a one- to two-notch credit-rating downgrade. The repricing is strongest for banks with tighter post-stress capital positions and stronger environmental orientation, yet higher spreads do not translate into subsequent reductions in emissions. These findings align with our state-dependent lending model, which adapts the intermediary asset pricing perspective to credit by linking loan risk premia to intermediary capital scarcity.

title: Consumption Responses to Rising Mortgage Rates: Unpacking the Cash-Flow Channel of Monetary Policy
affiliations: University of Copenhagen - Department of Economics, , Danske Bank and University of Oxford - Oxford University Centre for Business Taxation

detail.title: Consumption Responses to Rising Mortgage Rates: Unpacking the Cash-Flow Channel of Monetary Policy

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We study the transmission of rising interest rates to consumption using granular customer data from a major bank in Denmark. We show that households with adjustable-rate mortgages gradually reduced spending and increased deposits as market rates soared in 2022 but made no further spending cuts when their mortgage rates eventually reset to a higher level in 2023-2024. These patterns are consistent with forward-looking households who respond to new information about future mortgage costs and use liquid buffers to smooth consumption. The cash-flow channel of monetary policy may therefore operate almost instantaneously even when mortgage rates reset with a significant lag.

title: Term Premia in China Sovereign Bonds

detail.title: Term Premia in China Sovereign Bonds
detail.abstract: This paper estimates term premia in China sovereign bonds and asks how far movements in the yield curve should be interpreted as revisions to expected future short rates rather than changes in compensation for bearing duration risk. I estimate a three-factor Gaussian affine term-structure model on monthly ChinaBond zero-coupon yields from one month to thirty years between October 2009 and March 2026. The model implies a term-premium component that is close to zero at the very short end and rises with maturity. The central empirical result is that the decomposition is not equally credible across the curve. At maturities from roughly one to six years, the expected-rate component tracks realized future short rates more closely than simple yield benchmarks, and the model-implied premium forecasts subsequent bond excess returns. At seven to ten years, the same evidence becomes weaker, less stable across subsamples, and more sensitive to observable curve slopes. The paper therefore contributes a disciplined estimate of China sovereign term premia together with explicit maturity-specific credibility margins. The main implication is that medium-maturity China yields contain separable expectations and risk-premium information, whereas the far long end is better interpreted as a benchmark pricing object than as a sharply identified measure of expected policy or duration risk.

title: Does Global Financial Transparency Improve Tax Compliance in Developing Countries?

detail.title: Does Global Financial Transparency Improve Tax Compliance in Developing Countries?

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: In a coordinated effort to curb tax evasion, governments systematically exchange information about bank accounts with foreign owners. We study the compliance effects of the policy in the context of South Africa using information reports on 1 million foreign bank accounts linked to income and audit data. We find that self-reported foreign income increased sharply and persistently at the onset of information exchange, but remained much below the true foreign income implied by the information reports. We explain the partial compliance response by showing that, contrary to standard theory of third-party reporting, the detection risk associated with non-compliance was modest.

title: Border Carbon Adjustments Revisited
affiliations: University of Oldenburg, University of Oldenburg, World Bank Group and University of Wisconsin-Madison

detail.title: Border Carbon Adjustments Revisited

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: To address concerns about competitiveness and carbon leakage, countries with ambitious climate policies are increasingly looking to combine unilateral carbon pricing with border carbon adjustments (BCA). BCA aim to create a level playing field between domestically regulated energy-intensive and trade-exposed industries and their competitors abroad by imposing charges on the (unpriced) carbon embodied in imports and (potentially) rebating carbon costs on exports. At the same time, BCA are seen as measures that may have protectionist motivation and shift the burden of climate policy onto poorer developing economies that bear less historical responsibility for climate change, have limited financial and technological capacity for decarbonization, and may depend on CO₂-intensive exports. For an informed policy debate, understanding how BCA alter the economic burden of unilateral emissions pricing across all countries is essential. However, quantitative impact estimates derived from ex-ante simulation analyses vary considerably in the applied economic literature due to divergent assumptions on key drivers whose relative importance is difficult to distinguish from the outset. Based on controlled simulations with a large-scale computable general equilibrium model of global trade and carbon use, this paper provides a systematic sensitivity analysis of three fundamental dimensions that determine the impacts of BCA: (i) the policy design of BCA; (ii) the price responsiveness of supply and demand; and (iii) the input-output data characterizing initial heterogeneities of production, consumption, and trade patterns across countries.

title: Challenges in Implementing the EU CAP New Delivery Model -The Bulgarian Case
affiliations: Institute of Agricultural Economics and Institute of Agricultural Economics

detail.title: Challenges in Implementing the EU CAP New Delivery Model -The Bulgarian Case

declarations.funderStatement: This study is funded by the Bulgarian Science Fund, the project "Agricultural land, green transformation, energy transition, digital environment", Contract No КП-06-Н96/2 from 9.12.2025.

detail.abstract: The New Delivery Model of the European Union's Common Agricultural Policy for 2023-2027 introduces a major shift toward decentralized governance, granting Member States greater flexibility to meet shared socioeconomic and environmental targets through unified National Strategic Plans. Key features include integrated Pillar I and II interventions, result-oriented annual reporting, mandatory eco-schemes, and digitalized satellite monitoring. Despite high expectations, Bulgarian and international research on the practical implementation challenges of this model remains scarce due to data gaps, short execution experiences, and shifting political focus toward the EU Green Deal and regional geopolitical crises. This book chapter addresses this research gap by providing an initial assessment of the challenges surrounding the CAP New Delivery Model within the Bulgarian context. A three-stage qualitative methodology was employed: an autoethnographic summary of the authors' direct experience in developing Bulgaria's Strategic Plan and SWOT analysis; 15 face-to-face in-depth interviews conducted in 2025 with institutional managers, agrarian producers, and independent experts; and a subsequent 7-expert Focus Group in 2026. By analyzing preparation, implementation, and monitoring dynamics alongside future shifts toward a National and Regional Partnership Plan, this study outlines critical strategic directions to optimize public interventions and stakeholder coordination for the next programming period.

title: Nowcasting Low-Income Countries Through Global Linkages
affiliations: and Johns Hopkins University

detail.title: Nowcasting Low-Income Countries Through Global Linkages

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Timely assessment of economic activity is crucial for effective policymaking at the national, regional, and global levels. However, many economies still do not publish GDP data at a quarterly basis, creating persistent information gaps. In 2025, 34% of economies publish only annual GDP statistics. This lack of higher-frequency and timely data is particularly restrictive for emerging market and developing economies, where economic volatility and spillover risks are often highest. The problem is more severe for historical data: only 42% of economies have quarterly GDP estimates for a period longer than 20 years. To address these gaps, this paper develops a model that estimates missing quarterly GDP series by leveraging global and regional economic interconnections. The method transforms sparse annual data into quarterly estimates by exploiting higher-frequency information from the rest of the world, enabling real-time policymaking in both data-scarce economies and in global-level discussions. Moreover, this method ensures internally consistent estimates of regional and global economic activity, allowing both top-down and bottom-up scenario analyses.

title: There Will Be Liquidity! But Will There Be Transmission?
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF) and

detail.title: There Will Be Liquidity! But Will There Be Transmission?

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper examines the impact of voluntary and involuntary excess liquidity on monetary policy effectiveness and inflation in Kazakhstan. Consistent with first-principles predictions, we find that voluntary liquidity held for precautionary motives is (i) negatively related to the opportunity cost of holding liquid assets and to the level of mandatory reserve requirements; (ii) positively related to average liquidity outflows, proxied by transactional demand for cash; and (iii) ambiguously affected by the magnitude and volatility of the business cycle. We further show that higher voluntary liquidity weakens monetary policy transmission and increases exchange rate pass-through to inflation. In contrast, involuntary liquidity hampers monetary policy effectiveness no matter its level and it increases average inflation primarily through its influence on the formation of inflation expectations. Overall, the results suggest that reforms aimed at reducing both forms of liquidity would enhance monetary policy effectiveness and, ceteris paribus, reduce inflation.

title: Peer Pressure
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF),  and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Peer Pressure

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper shows that sovereign bond spreads are shaped not only by absolute debt levels but also by a country’s relative debt position within its peer group. Using panel fixed effects for over 80 emerging and developing economies over 1993-2024, we find that relative debt—especially benchmarked by income and commodity status—has greater explanatory power for spreads than gross debt alone. A one–standard deviation increase in relative debt raises spreads by roughly 0.2–0.3 standard deviations, comparable in magnitude to global risk indicators. Similarly, a 10 percent increase in relative debt is associated with a 3.8 percent increase in sovereign spreads, all else equal. The effect of relative debt is state-dependent, being stronger in countries with better institutions, access to concessional lending, and during periods of low risk aversion and ample global liquidity. These results hold across alternative specifications, sample periods, methodologies, and controls, which underscores the comparative nature of investor assessments and the importance of benchmarking for fiscal policy, debt management, and international surveillance.

title: Decoding Fiscal Messaging
affiliations: Joint Vienna Institute and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Decoding Fiscal Messaging

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Fiscal policy has re-emerged as a central tool of macroeconomic stabilization, yet the way governments communicate fiscal choices remains poorly understood. This paper provides the first systematic analysis of fiscal communication across the G7 from 2000–2024. Using a new dataset of budget documents, ministerial speeches, and press communiqués, we examine the clarity, thematic content, and rhetorical tone of official fiscal statements through computational text-analysis methods. We uncover a structured but fragmented communication architecture. Technical documents emphasize sustainability and constraints; speeches underscore growth, fairness, and investment; and press releases distill policy packages into succinct signals. Despite rising expectations of transparency, fiscal language remains complex and often optimistically framed. These patterns reflect institutional design, political incentives, and macroeconomic conditions. Our findings highlight fiscal communication as an underappreciated dimension of economic governance, one that shapes expectations, conditions credibility, and warrants deeper integration into fiscal policy analysis.

title: The Application of the Existing Intellectual Property Regime in the Metaverse: The United Kingdom as a Case Study

detail.title: The Application of the Existing Intellectual Property Regime in the Metaverse: The United Kingdom as a Case Study
detail.abstract:
The 21st-century innovations have presented one challenge to law everywhere in the world - the catch-up challenge. As expected, regulations ought not to stifle innovation. From the thoughts of Neal Stephenson to the declaration of Meta (formerly Facebook), we are now

witnessing a technological evolution that requires a holistic approach from Intellectual Property (IP) practitioners across the globe. The IP community is already thinking of how IP will find relevance in the metaverse. To critically contribute to this discussion, this

dissertation traces the origins of the metaverse to its present-day status. It considers its entire setup and how the law could regulate the metaverse. Agreed that there is no metaverse-specific regulation yet both at the international and national level, we can adapt the current IP laws in the United Kingdom to regulate the metaverse components worthy of IP protection.

title: An Analytical Study Of The 8th Pay Commission And Its Consequences For Public Sector Employees And Pensioners

detail.title: An Analytical Study Of The 8th Pay Commission And Its Consequences For Public Sector Employees And Pensioners
detail.abstract: Central government employees and pensioners in India are no strangers to the expectations that surround a Pay Commission. But the 8th Central Pay Commission (CPC) has created a level of attention like no other in recent memory, and with reason to. This is one of the largest pay revision exercises in the country's administrative history, with more than 50 lakh serving employees and about 69 lakh pensioners awaiting their benefits 1. This is a detailed breakdown of everything that has already occurred, how the numbers may appear, and what you can reasonably expect over the coming months. A BRIEF HISTORY: WHY PAY COMMISSIONS MATTER In India, the Pay Commission system refers to a periodic review of the salaries, allowances, and pension schemes of employees of the central government. Each Pay Commission, constituted about once every ten years, is an exhaustive review of the emoluments structure, with its recommendations accepted, revised, or amended by the government before implementation. 2 The 7 th Pay Commission, implemented in January 2016, changed the pay landscape for government employees. It introduced a pay matrix, changed the fitment factor to 2.57, and increased the minimum basic pay from 7,000 per month to 18,000 per month. A decade later, when purchasing power in real terms has been eroded by inflation, housing prices have soared, and healthcare costs have also increased dramatically, a new revision is much needed.

title: Leveraging Non-traditional Data for Macroeconomic Nowcasting

detail.title: Leveraging Non-traditional Data for Macroeconomic Nowcasting

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Making informed policy decisions is contingent upon the availability of reliable and timely data. The use of non-traditional data has been shown to be a powerful tool for enabling policymakers to conduct robust nowcasting—the practice of estimating the current period’s economic indicator(s), ahead of official releases, using a wide range of macroeconomic and high-frequency data. This paper showcases how different types of non-traditional data, such as indices extracted from satellite imagery, Google Trends, and flight tracking information, can be leveraged to complement official statistics and monitor economic activity, and how these timely signals can be incorporated into nowcasting models to provide early estimates of key macroeconomic variables in Morocco. The approach is applied to agricultural gross value added, tourism revenues, and the unemployment rate. The results demonstrate that non-traditional data substantially improves nowcasting models by enhancing predictive accuracy and enabling the rapid generation of nowcast estimates prior to the release of official data.

detail.abstract:
Background: Health systems facing population ageing need scalable ways to maintain preventive contact with older adults who have multimorbidity while hospital capacity remains under pressure. It is not well established whether sustained community-based preventive contact before admission is associated with lower inpatient resource intensity among older adults who are eventually admitted. We examined this question in a province-wide linked-record cohort from Henan, China, using the National Essential Public Health Services (NEPHS) elderly health-management programme as a routine community-based preventive-care exposure.

Methods: We did a retrospective linked-record cohort study using public-hospital inpatient discharge records, the NEPHS elderly health-management registry, and patient identifier files from Henan Province between 2019 and 2024. The primary exposure was NEPHS enrolment before the index admission. The primary outcomes were total inpatient cost and length of stay. We estimated a primary population-level adjusted contrast in the full complete-covariate cohort, design-balanced contrasts using inverse-probability-of-treatment weighting (IPTW), overlap weighting, and propensity-score matching, and a within-person fixed-effects contrast among enrolment switchers. The Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) was examined as a candidate clinical pathway, including attenuation and mediation analyses.

Findings: The primary complete-covariate cohort included 19,425,809 admissions among 5,938,289 patients aged 65 years or older. In the primary adjusted model, NEPHS enrolment before admission was associated with an approximately 9·9% lower total inpatient cost and a 0·679-day shorter length of stay. Estimates from IPTW, overlap weighting, and propensity-score matching were broadly consistent in direction and magnitude. Within-person fixed-effects estimates among switchers were smaller, suggesting that residual between-person selection contributed to the population-level association. Attenuation and mediation analyses were consistent with CCI contributing to part of the observed association. Associations were stronger for admissions among the oldest adults, those with recorded comorbidity, and some insurance-defined groups, especially admissions covered by the New Rural Cooperative Medical Scheme (NRCMS).

Interpretation: Prior NEPHS enrolment was associated with lower per-admission inpatient cost and shorter length of stay among older adults admitted to public hospitals in Henan. These findings are consistent with a population-level preventive-care interpretation in which sustained community-based preventive contact may be most relevant for people with greater clinical need and for some insurance-defined groups. Causal claims, conclusions about aggregate expenditure, and confirmation of mediation pathways require prospective or quasi-experimental studies with richer clinical and quality-of-care outcomes.

detail.title: Volatility Disagreement in the Options Market
detail.abstract: We construct a novel stock-level measure of volatility disagreement as the cross-sectional dispersion of realized variance forecasts built from heterogeneous information sets and machine learning models. Sorting single-name delta-hedged straddles on this measure yields a long-short return of-5.14% per month, robust to known option return predictors and not subsumed by disagreement about first moments or the variance risk premium. A one-standarddeviation increase in volatility disagreement is associated with a 30% rise in option position opening. The cross-sectional patterns of our disagreement measure align with recent theoretical advances of beliefs and pricing of variance claims. Evidence on attention, ownership, and arbitrage costs is more consistent with mispricing than risk compensation.

detail.abstract: The rapid diffusion of machine learning techniques in financial and energy market research has coincided with a renewed emphasis on causal inference frameworks that deliver structurally interpretable and policy-relevant insights. Although these domains have developed extensively in parallel, their systematic integration remains limited and insufficiently mapped. This paper surveys the literature on the intersection of causal inference, energy finance, and machine learning. First, we conduct a bibliometric analysis using a systematic search strategy organized into three conceptual blocks: causal inference, energy finance, and machine learning. Second, we identify and synthesize the principal methodological commonalities across the selected studies. We classify contributions by their empirical settings and data structures, highlighting how causality is operationalized in data-driven energy finance applications. Third, we provide an indepth methodological overview of the main approaches employed in this literature.

title: Assessing Climate-Related Health Risks in Morocco: Towards an Econometric Data-Driven Early Warning System
affiliations: Ibn Tofail University and Ibn Tofail University

detail.title: Assessing Climate-Related Health Risks in Morocco: Towards an Econometric Data-Driven Early Warning System
detail.abstract: This article assesses climate-related health risks in Morocco by proposing an econometric data-driven early warning system. Using a Vector Autoregression (VAR) model applied to annual data from 2000 to 2020, we analyze the dynamic interactions between life expectancy (LE), CO₂ emissions, the overall health budget (BGS), the number of inhabitants per physician (NHM), and the number of inhabitants per healthcare facility (NHE). Stationarity tests confirm the stability of the series in logarithmic differences, and model diagnostics validate its specification.The results show that LE in Morocco exhibits high inertia, with more than 94% of its variance explained by its own past shocks. CO₂ emissions, although positively correlated with LE in descriptive analyses, account for only about 1.35% of the variance in LE over a ten-year horizon, with a delayed effect. The health budget (BGS) contributes moderately (approximately 2%), confirming the importance of public health investments. Impulse response functions reveal that CO₂ shocks do not have a significant immediate impact on LE, suggesting a relative resilience of Morocco's health system to climate variability during the study period, possibly mitigated by the country's low emission levels and energy transition policies.This work provides an operational econometric framework for monitoring the impact of climate and health variables. It highlights the predominance of structural health determinants and argues for the targeted integration of climate indicators into epidemiological surveillance systems, enabling proactive health policy adapted to environmental challenges.

title: Bivariate sudden stop analysis of equity and bond fund flows to emerging markets using isolation forest
affiliations: and Deutsche Bundesbank

detail.title: Bivariate sudden stop analysis of equity and bond fund flows to emerging markets using isolation forest

publicationDetails.journalName: Deutsche Bundesbank Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper applies machine learning methods and anomaly detection to sudden stop analysis of portfolio flows. Using the isolation forest methodology, univariate as well as bivariate sudden stops of equity and bond fund flows to emerging markets are generated. An anomaly score and an anomaly classification are provided. The results point to an increase in anomalous portfolio flows to emerging markets in recent years. In addition, the isolation forest methodology appears to yield better results than the traditional approach to sudden stop analysis in classifying anomalies connected with the recent capital flow volatility related to the outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic as well as the interest rate reversal in advanced economies in recent years. The bivariate approach to anomaly detection is better able to identify anomalous episodes of financial stress, where both equity and bond markets are simultaneously affected. Most of the classified anomalies are related to fund flow stops (i.e. simultaneous stops to both equity and bond flows) or surges (i.e. surges in both equity and bond flows). In general, univariate and bivariate anomaly detection using machine learning techniques can play an important part and lead to a better understanding of sudden stops and surges.

title: A Multidimensional Statistical Approach to Assessing the Effectiveness of Targeting Mechanisms for Household Vulnerability to Poverty in Tanzania: Evidence from the 2022 Tanzania Demographic and Health Survey (TDHS)
