detail.title: A Multidimensional Statistical Approach to Assessing the Effectiveness of Targeting Mechanisms for Household Vulnerability to Poverty in Tanzania: Evidence from the 2022 Tanzania Demographic and Health Survey (TDHS)
detail.abstract: The study employed a multidimensional statistical approach to assess the effectiveness of targeting mechanisms for household vulnerability to poverty in Tanzania. Currently, Tanzania employs a traditional hybrid (three-stage) targeting system that integrates community-based targeting, proxy means testing, and geographic testing to identify truly poor and vulnerable households. The study found that household vulnerability is primarily influenced by physical living conditions and asset ownership, with associated indicators such as housing floor quality, wall material quality, access to electricity, and durable asset ownership serving as the most significant predictors. Using model evaluation metrics such as accuracy, F1-score, inclusion, and exclusion errors, a comparative analysis of predictive models (Random Forest, Proxy Means Testing, Extreme Gradient Boosting) was also conducted; the Random Forest model outperformed Proxy Means Testing (representing hybrid targeting system) and Extreme Gradient Boosting models by achieving the highest F1-score and the lowest exclusion error, making it the most efficient tool for identifying poor and vulnerable households that genuinely meet eligibility criteria for social protection programs. Moreover, Moran’s I scatterplot showed that vulnerability in Tanzania is not randomly distributed or dispersed, but geographically clustered, and identified the Katavi region as a statistically significant hotspot for targeted policy interventions using the local indicators of spatial association (LISA) map. The study, then, concludes that incorporating modern machine learning models, such as Random Forest with spatial mapping, for significant clustering is crucial to enhancing the accuracy, equity, and efficiency of existing social protection programs in identifying truly vulnerable households in Tanzania.

title: CLIMATE MANAGEMENT STRATEGIES AND THEIR IMPACT ON SMALLHOLDER POULTRY SUSTAINABILITY AND POVERTY REDUCTION IN NIGERIA
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Lagos State University of Science and Technology

detail.title: CLIMATE MANAGEMENT STRATEGIES AND THEIR IMPACT ON SMALLHOLDER POULTRY SUSTAINABILITY AND POVERTY REDUCTION IN NIGERIA
detail.abstract: Purpose: Climate change poses a severe threat to Nigerian smallholder poultry production. This situation negatively affects poultry productivity, aggravates food insecurity, and amplifies,poverty vulnerability. This research evaluates the adaptation methods used by smallholder poultry farmers in Nigeria and their effectiveness in improving livelihoods.,Methodology: Using an exploratory research design, we employed a multistage sampling technique to select 360 farmers from the study area.,Findings: Cooperative membership and extension services played a crucial role in enabling the adoption of climate management strategies. Poultry farmers producing exclusively chicken meat had lower likelihoods of utilising extension services (0.224) and of being cooperative members (0.296) in adopting climate strategies, compared to those producing both live birds and eggs. 82% of poultry meat farmers were aware of climate management strategies. 88% of farmers have adopted climate management strategies, including technological innovations (such as water management), veterinary interventions (like vitamins and medicine), and traditional knowledge systems. These management strategies significantly reduced poverty among smallholder poultry farmers.,Practical implication: The study thus proposes establishing a Smallholder Poultry Innovation Platform to foster collaboration, accelerate the adoption of innovations, and promote sustainable, climate-resilient poultry production in Nigeria. The recommendation is to distribute climate management strategies to farmers through public awareness campaigns by established networks including extension services, input suppliers, and cooperatives. The study aligns with key global sustainable development goals focused on poverty reduction (SDG 1), hunger elimination (SDG 2), and climate action (SDG 13).

title: Temporal misalignment of income and nutrition in cash-crop food systems of Sub-Saharan Africa: Rethinking food security policy
affiliations: International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI), Wollo University and Ethiopian Public Health Institute

detail.title: Temporal misalignment of income and nutrition in cash-crop food systems of Sub-Saharan Africa: Rethinking food security policy
detail.abstract: Summary In many cash-crop economies across Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), increased agricultural income does not always translate into improved food security or nutrition. While the income-nutrition gap is a long-standing challenge, this paper identifies why modern climate volatility and the 'lumpiness' of the 2026 global commodity market have created a 'new seasonality' that requires shifting from yield-based metrics to temporally aligned nutritional benchmarks. This paper argues that this disconnect reflects a failure of temporal alignment within food systems, where the timing of income, food availability, and nutritional needs are poorly synchronized. Seasonal income concentration, limited capacity for consumption smoothing, and intra-household allocation dynamics interact to produce predictable cycles of vulnerability. These dynamics are further shaped by market seasonality, gender relations, and nutrition knowledge. Addressing food insecurity therefore requires moving beyond income-focused approaches toward strategies that improve how and when resources are converted into food and care. Strengthening financial practices, empowering women in decision-making, and aligning interventions with seasonal realities are critical for achieving sustained nutritional gains.

title: The Emissions Paradox of Green Hydrogen Quotas in Multi-Carrier Energy Hubs
affiliations: , Aalborg University, Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology (UNIST) and Ewha Womans University

detail.title: The Emissions Paradox of Green Hydrogen Quotas in Multi-Carrier Energy Hubs
detail.abstract: Green hydrogen quota policies are based on the assumption that mandating hydrogen production through renewable-energy-based electrolysis leads to a reduction in greenhouse-gas emissions. This study shows that, in integrated energy systems with shared renewable resources, this assumption can be violated and the quota can instead trigger a system-level CO2 paradox. The underlying mechanism, referred to here as renewable energy cannibalization, arises when the electrolyzer, under quota pressure, diverts clean electricity from other co-located uses and the resulting deficit is compensated through carbon-intensive electricity imports from the upstream grid. To quantify this effect, a multi-carrier energy hub with independent agents interconnected through electricity, heat, and hydrogen buses is designed, and its performance is evaluated within a centralized mixed-integer linear programming framework. The green hydrogen quota is modeled under both aggregate-matching and hourly-matching approaches, and its effect is examined across 99 combinations of quota level and renewable penetration. The results show that, under aggregate matching, renewable energy cannibalization can lead to a policy triple failure, simultaneously causing higher emissions and system cost together with a contraction of the hydrogen economy. Hourly matching shifts the paradox boundary by about 5 to 11 percentage points, but does not eliminate it. The results also show that the boundary between policy success and failure under the hydrogen quota follows an approximately linear relationship, and that a green hydrogen quota without proportionate expansion of renewable capacity can operate in reverse.

title: Spatial Inequities in Food Environments: A Predictive Machine Learning Framework for Auditing Obesogenic Landscapes and Chronic Metabolic Health in the United States

detail.title: Spatial Inequities in Food Environments: A Predictive Machine Learning Framework for Auditing Obesogenic Landscapes and Chronic Metabolic Health in the United States

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract: This paper presents a high-granularity spatial and quantitative data auditing framework to investigate the structural correlation between regional food environments - specifically the prevalence of ‘food swamps’ and adult metabolic health outcomes across the United States. Integrating cross-sectional data from the USDA Food Environment Atlas and the CDC Branded Food Products Database, I engineered an explicit geographic metric: the Food Swamp Ratio (FSR). To overcome the non-linear limitations of traditional ordinary least squares (OLS) regressions, an optimized XGBoost (Extreme Gradient Boosting) machine learning model was deployed to isolate predictive features driving regional adult obesity and type 2 diabetes indices. The model identifies that a high FSR exerts a statistically superior predictive weight over standalone economic factors, such as median household income. The findings demonstrate that public health interventions targeting physical food infrastructure carry significant policy efficacy for systemic cost containment within federal healthcare frameworks.

title: The Tradability Filter: Endogenous No-Trade Bands and Executable Edge in Prediction Markets
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Tradability Filter: Endogenous No-Trade Bands and Executable Edge in Prediction Markets
detail.abstract: Prediction-market prices are often interpreted as direct probabilities of future events. This interpretation is useful for forecasting, but it is not equivalent to a trading opportunity. A probability-price gap becomes economically meaningful only if it survives execution prices, fees, bid-ask spreads, order-book depth, model uncertainty, settlement risk, adverse selection, and capital lock-up. This paper develops a theoretical framework for binary event contracts that separates forecast accuracy, expected value, and executable profit. I adapt the Glosten-Milgrom model to binary event contracts and derive closed-form competitive bid and ask quotes under informed order flow. The resulting adverse-selection spread is increasing in the share of informed flow and is largest for events near probability one half. The paper then distinguishes semantic event risk from settlement risk. When informed traders observe the semantic event while the contract settles on a noisy outcome, settlement ambiguity attenuates the adverse-selection component of the spread by the factor (1-delta_0-delta_1). Asymmetric settlement errors also shift the no-trade band: false-positive settlement risk raises it, while false-negative settlement risk lowers it. The framework formalizes when apparent prediction-market mispricing becomes tradable edge.

title: Machine Learning and Dynamic Capabilities: A Qualitative Analysis of Resilience, Risk, and Sustainability in Taiwan's Semiconductor Supply Chains
affiliations: University of Plymouth and University of Plymouth

detail.title: Machine Learning and Dynamic Capabilities: A Qualitative Analysis of Resilience, Risk, and Sustainability in Taiwan's Semiconductor Supply Chains
detail.abstract: This study examines how machine learning (ML) enhances resilience, risk management, and sustainability within Taiwan's semiconductor supply chains (SSCs). Whilst existing research tends to address these dimensions in isolation, their interdependencies within complex, data-intensive production systems remain underexplored. Drawing on Dynamic Capabilities Theory (DCT) and qualitative data from eleven semi-structured interviews with industry professionals in Taiwan, this article investigates how ML is adopted, interpreted, and embedded within organisational routines. The findings reveal that ML functions as a dynamic capability amplifier, augmenting managerial cognition across sensing, seizing, and transforming processes rather than supplanting human judgement. Effectiveness is contingent upon data governance, infrastructural maturity, and cross-tier coordination. To synthesise these insights, the study develops the AI-Enhanced Semiconductor Supply Chain Framework (AI-SSCF), offering theoretical and practical guidance for responsible ML deployment. The article contributes to DCT scholarship by conceptualising cognitive hybridity as central to capability renewal in high-velocity industries.

title: The Invisible Ingredient: A Framework for AI Labor Composition Transparency in Commerce
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Invisible Ingredient: A Framework for AI Labor Composition Transparency in Commerce

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Independent Researcher with passion for innovation and technology.
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract:
Consumer product labeling has evolved over decades to encode what markets, on their own, fail to disclose: what is in a product, where it came from, and how it was made. A new dimension of product and service provenance now goes undisclosed in virtually every commercial transaction: the proportion of human versus automated labor used to create it.

This paper proposes AI Labor Composition Transparency (ALCT), an original regulatory framework requiring registered businesses to publish the ratio of human labor hours to Normalized AI Processing Units (NAPUs) used in the production of goods and services, benchmarked by industry, role, and product category. Products and services meeting a defined human-effort threshold would carry a verifiable Human-Made designation, administered through FTC authority and NIST measurement standards.

Extensive research confirms no existing federal, state, or international regulatory framework — including the EU AI Act Article 50 — addresses product-level AI labor composition disclosure. ALCT fills that gap. The paper analyzes the constitutional framework under Zauderer and NIFLA v. Becerra, the jurisdictional structure across goods and regulated services, the token normalization problem and its proposed solution, small business impact thresholds, WTO compatibility considerations, and the phased voluntary-to-mandatory implementation pathway modeled on GAAP financial reporting development. The argument is not that automation is harmful. It is that transparent markets require transparent inputs.

detail.title: Competition in Digital Financial Services – Regulatory Strategies and Pathways for Emerging Markets and Developing Economies

publicationDetails.detailsText: Cambridge Centre for Alternative Finance Research Paper No. 68

detail.abstract: The report considers how policy and regulatory tools can be leveraged to promote competition in digital financial services (DFS) in emerging market and developing economies (EMDEs) and in particular their relation to capital formation. The study focuses on four interlinked areas. It first proposes a conceptual framework to help public and financial authorities prioritise competition-enhancing interventions based on their jurisdictional market and regulatory context, policy objectives, and the intended scope of action. Building on this conceptual framework, the report maps these tools to supply- and demand-side competition barriers, offering practical guidance to regulators on how to prioritise interventions based on the most prominent competition constraints in their respective jurisdictional context. Barriers to private capital formation are then examined, and related to specific competition challenges and tools, equipping regulators and policymakers with a stronger conceptual foundation for designing interventions that can support greater capital formation through more competitive DFS markets. A comparative case study analysis is then undertaken, to assess the impact of selected competition-enhancing regulatory initiatives on DFS markets across countries in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) and the Asia-Pacific (APAC) region. This comparative approach helps mitigate the limitations of single-jurisdiction case studies, where isolating the impact of an initiative from other influencing factors is often challenging. Finally, the report synthesises key lessons for developing strategies to support competition in DFS markets, recognizing that public and financial authorities do not always have an explicit competition mandate.

title: The Real Effects of Payment Anonymity: Evidence from the Crypto Ecosystem

detail.title: The Real Effects of Payment Anonymity: Evidence from the Crypto Ecosystem

publicationDetails.journalName: INSEAD Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Does the design of payment systems cause real welfare consequences? Despite the rapid growth of cryptocurrency, the welfare effects of anonymous digital payments remain empirically unknown. I study the staggered rollout of over 30,000 Bitcoin ATMs across U.S. counties, kiosks that convert cash to cryptocurrency with minimal identification, as a laboratory for estimating these consequences. BTM entry increases total crime by 6.9 percent, with effects concentrated in offenses that exploit anonymity, irreversibility, and cash-to-crypto conversion, while crimes unrelated to payment design barely respond. Tracing the causal chain further, BTM entry fuels local drug markets and raises overdose mortality. Crime-induced losses erode household balance sheets, raising credit delinquency in affected neighborhoods. These harms are regressive. Minority and Hispanic communities, young adults, and areas with weaker financial infrastructure absorb the largest increases in victimization and the steepest declines in financial health, simultaneously widening pre-existing inequality in safety, public health, and credit access. To scale these local effects to the aggregate level, I first use on-chain forensic analysis to trace BTM-originated funds along their downstream paths, identifying the routing intermediaries each transaction passes through and the share that terminates at illicit endpoints. I then build an informational model in which anonymity at each stage weakens transaction traceability and raises social harm. Calibrated to these on-chain flow shares, the model translates the local causal estimates into aggregate welfare statements, yielding a national-level measure of the cost generated by anonymous payment infrastructure.

detail.abstract: Aggregate stock prices and aggregate consumption share a common stochastic trend. We estimate this long-run relation in real time and recover a price-consumption cycle that captures transitory deviations of stock prices from their consumption-implied value. These deviations mean-revert over business-cycle horizons and predict future returns on the aggregate market and characteristic-sorted portfolios, both in-and out-of-sample, from one quarter to two years ahead. The cycle does not forecast consumption growth, and its predictive power disappears when consumption is excluded from the long-run relation. The evidence suggests that consumption anchors aggregate asset prices and that departures from this anchor reveal time-varying expected returns.

title: Allocating the remaining global CO2 budget within Absolute Environmental Sustainability Assessment: A Decent Living Standards approach
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Allocating the remaining global CO2 budget within Absolute Environmental Sustainability Assessment: A Decent Living Standards approach
detail.abstract: Allocating the remaining global CO2 budget is a central challenge for sustainability science as the available carbon space is finite and its distribution is inherently contested. While Absolute Environmental Sustainability Assessment provides a framework for assessing activities against ecological carrying capacities, the social basis on which these capacities should be allocated remains underdeveloped. In particular, Decent Living Standards and carbon-allocation approaches have rarely been operationally integrated. This paper aims to address this gap by developing a Decent Living Standards-based allocation framework for the remaining global CO2 budget. Empirically, the study constructs a country-level Decent Living Standards index based on a multidimensional set of indicators covering health care, education, housing, consumption, information and communication, and mobility. This index is then used to implement a prioritarian allocation rule that distributes the remaining global CO2 budget according to countries’ observed shortfalls from minimum decent living conditions. The rule is explicitly needs-sensitive, but it does not adjust for governance quality or unequal internal distribution of the benefits from past resource use. The results show that the choice of allocation principle has major distributive consequences. While equal per capita allocation distributes carbon space largely according to population size, the Decent Living Standards-based rule produces a substantial redistribution toward countries with lower Decent Living Standards attainment. The findings demonstrate that carbon-budget allocation depends strongly on whether fairness is defined in terms of equal shares or need fulfilment, and they highlight the importance of integrating minimum social standards into assessments of ecological scarcity.

title: Courts, Regulators, and the Hallucination Problem: How Canadian Law Is Responding to Large Language Models in Legal Submissions

detail.title: Courts, Regulators, and the Hallucination Problem: How Canadian Law Is Responding to Large Language Models in Legal Submissions

contentType.other: Article accepted, pending publication in the Alberta Law Review Volume 64, Issue 3

detail.abstract: The rapid integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into the Canadian legal profession has introduced significant challenges to the administration of justice, most notably the phenomenon of artificial intelligence "hallucinations" resulting in the submission of fabricated legal authorities to courts. This article provides a comprehensive analysis of how Canadian courts and regulators in common law jurisdictions have responded to this disruption over a critical three-year period following the release of ChatGPT. Examining the evolving regulatory landscape, the article traces the development of early judicial interventions, including the Alberta Tri-Court Notice and the Federal Court’s distinct mandatory disclosure regime, alongside guidance documents published by various provincial Law Societies and the Canadian Bar Association. It further reviews pivotal Canadian jurisprudence—such as Zhang v. Chen, Reddy v. Saroya, and Ko v. Li—to illustrate a discernible shift from initial judicial leniency toward increasingly stringent enforcement mechanisms, including personal cost awards and contempt proceedings. The analysis identifies core systemic themes, particularly the universal imposition of a non-delegable duty of human verification ("human in the loop") anchored within existing professional obligations of competence, confidentiality, and candour. Finally, the article highlights critical under-examined tensions within the current framework, including the serious access-to-justice implications of holding self-represented litigants to strict verification standards without institutional support, and the regulatory distinction between free consumer chatbots and enterprise-grade legal AI platforms. Ultimately, the author argues that while Canada’s regulatory posture favours managed technological integration over prohibition, the enduring efficacy of relying on traditional ethical frameworks to govern rapidly advancing generative tools remains an open question for the justice system.

title: Spectral Geometry of Attritional Combat Extending the Lanchester-Osipov Framework: Phase-Space Analysis and Decision Support
affiliations: and University of the German Federal Armed Forces - Helmut Schmidt Universität

detail.title: Spectral Geometry of Attritional Combat Extending the Lanchester-Osipov Framework: Phase-Space Analysis and Decision Support
detail.abstract: This article develops a unified analytical treatment of attritional combat dynamics incorporating mutual attrition and intrinsic decay. Extending the classical Lanchester-Osipov equations, the fully coupled 2 × 2 system is analysed through spectral invariants and phasespace geometry. A Lorentzian metric and associated quadratic invariants are employed to classify dynamical régimes and terminal outcomes. Closed-form criteria for victory, defeat, and stalemate are derived together with explicit engagement-duration expressions. The conservative case appears as a Hamiltonian limit recovering the N-Square Law, while a degenerate limit yields the unaimed re-formulation as a Lotka-Volterra reduction. Reinforcements are interpreted as impulsive state interventions within a hybrid-systems framework, allowing outcome assessment through invariant structure rather than simulation. The approach is illustrated through a retrospective analysis of the Battle of Iwo Jima.

title: ASEAN’s Trade and Investment in a Fragmented World

detail.title: ASEAN’s Trade and Investment in a Fragmented World

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper examines the short- and medium-term effects of the 2018–19 China-U.S. tariff increases on the trade and investment flows of ASEAN member economies. Using granular trade data, we demonstrate that several ASEAN countries experienced a disproportionate growth in exports of products that were targeted by these tariffs. To further explore the dynamic and often immediate responses of international capital flows to these trade policy shifts, we leverage a novel firm-level FDI database that allows us to identify surges in sectoral investment inflows. Among ASEAN countries, Vietnam stands out as the one where FDI in targeted sectors grew notably faster during 2018–19, likely contributing to its observed export gains over the medium term. At the same time, our analysis reveals that trade gains in targeted products have not universally translated into stronger overall export performance across ASEAN. More generally, while trade reallocation may yield short- and medium-term gains, these gains can be offset over time by the higher long-term aggregate losses associated with trade fragmentation.

title: Political Fragility

detail.title: Political Fragility

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This study uses an entropy balancing model to show that coups d’état can reduce GDP growth by around 2.3 percentage points in the same year. This is a larger effect than some previous estimates, and is found to be persistent over time, reducing cumulative GDP growth by around five percentage points over the following five years. This study goes deeper than previous research into the drivers of that impact, finding that economic sanctions are an an important reason for the observed lower growth in many cases and that the principal channel is via private consumption and investment.

detail.abstract: High-debt euro area economies face fiscal consolidation in a low-growth environment. We use a Heterogeneous Agent New Keynesian model to assess how consolidation composition shapes aggregate and distributional outcomes in a representative high-debt economy. The status quo is not neutral: delay generates its own costs through lower investment, higher debt service, and damage to constrained households. For a given fiscal effort, expenditure-based consolidation achieves faster debt reduction with lower growth and distributional costs than revenue-based consolidation. As a complementary exercise, pairing the expenditurebased path with growth-enhancing structural reforms further improves outcomes by lifting real wages, a channel that disproportionately benefits hand-to-mouth households. Across both strategies, modest well targeted transfers to low-income households can substantially mitigate distributional costs at minimal fiscal expense while supporting aggregate demand.

detail.abstract: Government securities-backed repo markets constitute a key funding source for market participants in many jurisdictions. A number of recent stress episodes, e.g., in US and UK repo markets, has led to renewed efforts to strengthen the resilience of repo markets. This notably includes a push to increased central clearing via central counterparties (CCPs) which may come via market incentives or in the form of mandatory clearing. Central clearing is commonly considered as a key tool to increase transparency and understanding of markets and improve the risk management practices of market participants. This paper provides a brief overview of post trade-arrangements in select government securities repo markets and offers a structured analysis of potential benefits and risks of bringing repo markets onto centrally cleared platforms from a CCP perspective. The paper lists a set of key considerations that CCPs—and indirectly—policy makers could take into account when exploring the expansion of repo clearing services or opting for a repo clearing mandate. Aside from considerations pertaining to access modalities to repo clearing services, default management and market structure-related aspects are of key importance. Together, these factors ensure that the transition of repo transactions from a decentralized, uncleared set-up to central clearing is conducive to more resilient repo and ultimately government bond markets.

title: 5G Signal Propagation: Deriving Ideal Path Loss Constant for Indian Cities

detail.title: 5G Signal Propagation: Deriving Ideal Path Loss Constant for Indian Cities
detail.abstract:
Accurate radio propagation modeling is critical for efficient 5G network planning, particularly in environments where standard path-loss assumptions may not adequately represent local terrain and construction characteristics. Existing propagation models, including the Okumura-Hata model, were largely developed using measurements from non-Indian environments and may therefore introduce inaccuracies when applied to Indian urban settings.

This study investigates the path-loss exponent across representative Indian rural, semi-urban, and dense urban environments using field measurements collected in Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh, India. Measured signal strengths were compared against predictions generated by the Okumura-Hata model to determine environment-specific deviations and derive correction factors. The analysis demonstrates that distinct habitation classes exhibit measurable differences in propagation behavior, resulting in varying path-loss exponents and coverage predictions.

The findings indicate that the incorporation of locally derived path-loss corrections can significantly improve the alignment between predicted and observed signal strengths. While limited in geographical scope, the study provides a practical framework for enhancing empirical radio network planning and offers a foundation for future large-scale investigations into Indian 5G propagation characteristics. The methodology may assist telecom operators, network planners, and researchers in developing more accurate coverage estimation models for next-generation wireless networks.

This paper is derived from the author's Master's Dissertation completed at BITS Pilani (2021).

detail.title: Factors Related to Consumers' Preferences of Fast-Food Products in Bangladesh: A Case Study
detail.abstract: Fast food is a high growing industrial sector of Bangladesh as it is concerned with the tastes and habits of the people. The food-taking habit has been changing very fast among the people of Dhaka-the capital city of Bangladesh over last decade. The reasons could be attributed by the increase of awareness, growth of education, development of information technology, and expansion of television and print media in Bangladesh. This paper aims at identifying the preference factors of fast food consumers living in Dhaka city. This study was conducted among the university students who are used to take fast food at their leisure time. To conduct the study, a total of 250 respondents were interviewed with a structured questionnaire. Both descriptive and inferential statistics were used in analyzing the data. Multivariate analysis like factor analysis was performed to identify the preference factors of the fast food consumer. Multiple regressions were conducted to identify the relationship between the factors identified through factor analysis and the overall measure of preference of the consumers. Results show that the consumers give most importance on brand reputation of the fast food followed by closeness and accessibility, similar taste of fast food, cost and quality relationship, discount & taste, clean and hygiene, salesmanship and decoration, fat & cholesterol, and self-service. This study suggests that the brand reputation, closeness and accessibility, similar taste of fast food, and cost and quality relationship might be emphasized to improve the attraction of the university students towards fast food at Dhaka city.

detail.abstract:
This paper introduces the Legal Tender Closure Gap Doctrine, a legal and constitutional framework for analyzing cryptocurrency payment use beyond conventional securities, commodities, property, and tax classifications. The doctrine argues that the central question in cryptocurrency law is not merely what a token is, but what legal function the transaction asks the token to perform. When cryptocurrency is sold as part of an investment arrangement, securities law may properly apply. When traded through market infrastructure, commodities and market-integrity frameworks may be implicated. When held, exchanged, or disposed of, property and tax law remain relevant. But when cryptocurrency or stablecoins are used directly as payment for goods, services, wages, invoices, private obligations, or commercial settlement, the transaction enters a distinct legal posture: private settlement without sovereign monetary closure.

The paper defines legal-tender closure as sovereign-recognized monetary finality: the point at which an obligation is discharged within the lawful monetary order rather than merely accepted, recorded, taxed, regulated, or privately settled. It argues that private parties may accept crypto payment, and law may recognize contract performance, tax consequences, compliance obligations, or commercial-law effects, without converting the payment instrument into legal tender or sovereign money. The doctrine therefore preserves four distinctions: accepted is not closed; transferred is not discharged; valued is not money; and settlement is not legal tender.

Building across constitutional monetary authority, federal legal-tender law, securities and commodities precedent, IRS digital-asset treatment, FinCEN and OFAC guidance, U.C.C. commercial-law developments, stablecoin policy, Federal Reserve settlement architecture, and long-horizon systemic-risk analysis, the paper shows how private payment functionality may create unresolved public consequences at scale. These consequences include payroll-tax residue, public-revenue friction, bank-deposit migration, monetary-policy transmission risk, stablecoin reserve fragility, sanctions and AML/BSA degradation, dollar-centrality pressure, government-continuity exposure, consumer and commercial-law fragmentation, and reactive sovereign-recognition pressure.

The doctrine is not anti-crypto. It is anti-conceptual collapse. It permits lawful innovation while insisting that private settlement, regulatory recognition, and sovereign monetary closure remain analytically distinct. Its concluding claim is that the greatest long-horizon risk is not that cryptocurrency fails as payment. It is that cryptocurrency succeeds as private payment while failing as sovereign closure. That gap — between private acceptance and legal-tender finality — is the legal architecture this doctrine names.

title: The Chokepoint Friction: An Institutional Model of Non-Reserve Settlement Traps in the Strait of Hormuz

detail.title: The Chokepoint Friction: An Institutional Model of Non-Reserve Settlement Traps in the Strait of Hormuz
detail.abstract: This paper constructs a pure Coasean institutional framework to evaluate the macroeconomic frictions that emerge when a localized transit authority mandates non-reserve currency settlement within a critical maritime trade corridor. Specifically, we model a theoretical mechanism where the Persian Gulf Strait Authority mandates that commercial vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz clear transit tolls exclusively in non-convertible Chinese Renminbi (RMB). We demonstrate that the strategic de-dollarization of a physical maritime choke point does not inherently destabilize the monetary primacy of the global hegemon. Instead, it functions as an asymmetric transaction cost trap for neighboring trade hubs. By exploiting an absolute geographic monopoly, the mandate imposes severe currency mismatches and structural settlement traps that drain the foreign exchange sovereign reserves of neighboring nations, directly destabilizing the fixed currency pegs that underpin the regional financial architecture.

title: What makes Strategic Transformation Programmes Successful? Evidence from Central Europe
affiliations: University of Oxford

detail.title: What makes Strategic Transformation Programmes Successful? Evidence from Central Europe
detail.abstract:
This study examines strategic transformation programmes and investigates what makes some of these initiatives more successful than others. Based on evidence from Central Europe, the research explores how strategic concepts, change management and programme management interact in the delivery of complex organisational transformation. It draws on eleven semi-structured interviews and twenty-five surveys with managers involved in strategic transformation programmes.
 
The findings highlight several areas that influence the perceived success of transformation efforts, including clear vision and strategy, communication, leadership, stakeholder commitment, realistic planning, flexibility and people-related aspects of change. The study also shows that organisations make different choices when structuring transformation programmes, and that the most appropriate approach depends on organisational context, strategic goals and managerial preferences. 

The research argues that strategic transformation should not be treated as the domain of a single managerial discipline. Instead, successful transformation requires the alignment of strategic intent, programme structure, change management, communication, leadership and strategy execution. By organising these issues into a practical set of managerial areas, the study contributes to the discussion on strategic transformation, organisational change, change management and programme management in a way that can support both academic reflection and business practice.

title: Of Mice, Men and Machines: A Future Direction for Legal Personhood
affiliations: Deakin Law School

detail.title: Of Mice, Men and Machines: A Future Direction for Legal Personhood
detail.abstract: Law personifies its subjects. Once a legal person, certain rights, duties and obligations follow. At least that is the standard picture; but that picture is somewhat incomplete. The orthodox view of legal personhood is that it requires no necessary connection with human personhood; the legal person is simply whomever, or whatever, law says it is. And recently, the law has had quite a lot to say on expanding these conceptual boundaries. Examples include conferring legal personhood on a range of natural phenomena (such as rivers, mountains, and mother nature), movements to extend legal personhood to animals, as well as related but adjacent conversations about the appropriate legal recognition for AI. Such instances require careful consideration of the nature and scope of legal personhood in order that we may pursue its coherent and principled development. This article makes a modest case for how we might do so.

detail.abstract: Agentic AI systems are moving from experimental deployment to critical infrastructure, yet the field's dominant safety and governance approaches operate at the model level-alignment at training, moderation at output, and policy at regulation. This paper proposes that trustworthy AI at infrastructure scale requires governance woven into the architecture itself: into how operations are authorized before execution, how systems survive degradation, how identity and provenance are established at inference time, and how failure is measured continuously. WHYTL is a research program of eleven interdependent components, developed under WHYLD (the research division of XWHYZ), that together constitute a constraint-first stack for sovereign-grade AI infrastructure. Anchored by the Sovereign Behavioral Lag (SBL) thesis-the structural delay between AI capability advancement and sovereign institutional response-the program spans five architectural layers: Governance, Execution Control, Infrastructure and Resilience, Identity and Provenance, and Measurement and Certification. This paper maps the program, situates it against prior art, identifies genuine novel contributions, and provides entry points for safety researchers, policy practitioners, and infrastructure architects.

title: Cultural Distortion in the Going-Global of Zhejiang's Cultural New Three Categories: A Five-stage Analytical Framework Based on Encoding-Decoding Theory

detail.title: Cultural Distortion in the Going-Global of Zhejiang's Cultural New Three Categories: A Five-stage Analytical Framework Based on Encoding-Decoding Theory
detail.abstract: This study examines cultural distortion in the going-global of Zhejiang's "cultural new three categories"-web literature, web drama, and web games-through Hall's encoding-decoding theory. It defines cultural distortion as the systematic mismatch between producers' encoded meanings and overseas audiences' decoding positions, leading to the weakening, transformation, or reversal of intended cultural meanings. To address this problem, the study constructs a fivestage analytical framework consisting of encoding, text, circulation, decoding, and reproduction. Based on exploratory materials from public comments and platform-visible discussions across web fiction, web drama, and web game cases, it proposes four types of distortion: symbolic distortion, narrative distortion, value distortion, and platform re-encoding distortion. The preliminary analysis suggests that negotiated decoding occupies a substantial share of audience responses, while platform mediation and algorithmic visibility further reshape cultural interpretation. The study also develops a hierarchical governance framework based on probability, impact scope, severity, and reversibility. It contributes an exploratory model for identifying, tracing, and governing cultural distortion in provincial cultural going-global practice, and offers policy-oriented implications for Zhejiang's digital cultural governance and international communication. AI-assisted tools were used only for language polishing and improving the clarity of expression.

detail.abstract: This study examines the livelihood forms of the Loinang people in Central Sulawesi that have become increasingly integrated into market mechanisms, generating profound socioecological transformations within the community. Adopting a socio-historical perspective, the research aims to identify how and through what processes these changes have unfolded. The study employs a qualitative approach grounded in an interpretive paradigm. Data were collected through participant observation, in-depth interviews with fifteen key informants, focus group discussions (FGDs), and an analysis of official documents and academic literature. The data were analyzed using a thematic method supported by NVivo software, enabling systematic coding, thematic mapping, and visualization of relationships among themes. The validity of the findings was strengthened through triangulation of sources, methods, and time. The findings reveal that prior to permanent settlement (nomadic subsistence phase), the Loinang people relied primarily on hunting and gathering, shifting cultivation, and direct subsistence consumption from natural resources. Following sedentarization (sedentary livelihood phase), their economic practices transformed into market-oriented agriculture centered on rice, maize, and vegetable commodities. This shift has directly contributed to improved food security, the emergence of clearly stratified patterns of land ownership, and increasing ecological pressure. Moreover, social relations within the Loinang community have become more competitive and individualistic, social differentiation has intensified, and the majority of livelihood needs are now mediated by market mechanisms.

title: Hold Back, Team Up, or Take Over? Optimal Timing of AI Access
affiliations: University of Michigan, Stephen M. Ross School of Business and University of Michigan, Stephen M. Ross School of Business

detail.title: Hold Back, Team Up, or Take Over? Optimal Timing of AI Access
detail.abstract: When should a firm withhold AI access from an employee, allow human-AI collaboration, or take the project over with AI? We study this question in a continuous-time principal-agent model of stochastic project completion with hidden effort and privately observed success. The principal chooses success rewards, the timing of AI access, and termination among three modes: human-only work, human-AI collaboration, and principal-run AI. The optimal contract has an ordered phase structure: the phases always appear in the order human-only work, human-AI collaboration, and principal-run AI, but any phase may have zero duration. We characterize the optimal policy in all primitive parameter regions: the firm may use principal-run AI immediately, rely on human-only work before AI takeover, begin with collaboration before takeover, or use all three phases for positive duration. This contrasts with the first-best static operating benchmark, in which effort and reporting are contractible and the principal uses a single mode with the highest static operating value. The structure of the optimal contract yields several implications. Upon granting AI access the worker's success reward decreases; a higher shirking benefit for human component accelerates AI access; a more capable standalone AI can delay and shorten collaboration; and allowing collaboration can reduce the worker's initial information rent. We also characterize the optimal contract in presence of shadow AI: unauthorized AI tools that the agent can use before the firm authorizes AI access. Shadow AI has two forms: a cheap shadow tool that complements human input and a costly firm-grade shadow tool that can be privately financed only by diverting enough project resources.

title: Provable Institutional Control for Tokenized Finance

detail.title: Provable Institutional Control for Tokenized Finance
detail.abstract:
The first generation of programmable finance optimized transactional throughput and settlement mechanics. While distributed ledger platforms demonstrated the viability of automated ownership tracking, institutional adoption remains severely constrained by a critical structural disconnect: the transaction execution plane has achieved near-instantaneous velocity, while the accompanying governance, risk management, and authorization frameworks remain manual, fragmented, and lagging. This paper identifies this asymmetry as the "Governance Bottleneck," arguing that the primary scalability challenge in institutional digital finance resides not in transaction execution, but in continuous, cross-organizational governance synchronization.

We reframe financial networks as architectures for propagating structural compliance and legal enforceability rather than merely transferring digital value. Through an operational risk assessment of major structural collapses—including FTX, Celsius, and Terra/Luna—this paper demonstrates that systemic crises originate from fragile governance topography and opaque authorization pathways rather than defects in settlement infrastructure. These case studies prove that transaction execution engines can function flawlessly while underlying fiduciary and asset segregation boundaries simultaneously fail, introducing unmonitored counterparty and contagion risks.

To mitigate these exposures, this paper introduces a non-disruptive, backward-compatible control plane architecture based on Programmable Institutional Control (PIC) and Governance Synchronization. This framework shifts the enterprise risk paradigm from retrospective, post-hoc auditing to automated, ex-ante enforcement. By evaluating regulatory constraints, multi-signature mandates, and commercial law perimeters (such as UCC Article 12) in real time prior to ledger mutation, this architecture delivers a machine-verifiable control plane capable of ensuring zero-fail compliance continuity.

detail.abstract:
The International Business (IB) discipline persistently looks for key concepts that can legitimise its existence as a separate scientific discipline in at least two related areas of research: (1) management sciences, and (2) international (political) economics. A key concept, thereby, is arguably that of 'distance'.

Rather than arguing which single aspect of distance should prevail in management practice, it seems more important to argue in favour of a more integrative approach to distance—from the premise that MNE managers have to take all dimensions of distance into account, preferably simultaneously. This presents a very complex challenge. This paper aims to set the scene for such an approach by distinguishing the dimensions of distance covered by extant research as published in leading IB journals, in order to present a richer and more meaningful framework for managing distance. On the basis of such an approach, managers should be able to prioritise those distance dimensions that are of particular relevance to their business. I call this the ‘Strategic Distance Fit’ challenge.

detail.title: Sovereignty Without a Name: The CEO as Feudal Lord
detail.abstract: This paper argues that the modern chief executive at sufficient scale occupies a structurally equivalent position to the feudal lord in three specific senses: in directing the means of production at societal scale, in the practical constraint of exit available to those whose labor sustains the system, and in the exercise of quasi-sovereign power over the legal and regulatory conditions governing their own conduct. A fourth condition, the ceiling on concentrated power imposed by geography and military competition under feudalism, is shown to be absent in the present case, suggesting that the historical analogy, rather than overstating the problem, may understate it. The paper extends the author's prior framework on the Principle of Concentrated Control (Dickinson, 2025) into explicitly political territory, focusing on the corporate form itself as a legal technology of exemption and on platform monopolies as a novel form of private sovereignty without territorial limit. The argument is structural, not rhetorical.

title: Measuring Racial Disparities in Rent Growth Under Algorithmic Landlord Concentration in U.S. Metros

detail.title: Measuring Racial Disparities in Rent Growth Under Algorithmic Landlord Concentration in U.S. Metros
detail.abstract: The 2024 Department of Justice antitrust complaint against RealPage, Inc. named five major residential REITs for coordinating algorithmic rent pricing across hundreds of thousands of apartment units in major US metropolitan areas. This paper studies whether census-tract-level corporate landlord concentration (CLC), measured from SEC EDGAR 10-K property filings geocoded to census tracts, the first such application in the literature, is associated with rent growth 2019-2023, and whether that association is larger in majority-minority neighborhoods. Rent outcomes are measured using the Zillow Observed Rent Index (ZORI). To account for the possibility that corporate landlords preferentially locate in neighborhoods already seeing rent appreciation, all regressions control for a fully novel Algorithmic Housing Burden Index (AHBI), a composite of pre-existing rent burden and market tightness from ACS data. Across 665 census tracts in ten US metropolitan areas, doubling REIT concentration is associated with 2.8 percentage points higher rent growth (p = 0.086, p = 0.030, HC1 robust). This association is significantly stronger in majority-minority tracts. Within the same metro, high-CLC majority-minority tracts are associated with 5.9 percentage points higher rent growth than comparable white tracts (p = 0.039). An XGBoost model predicts 44 percent of out-of-sample rent growth variance, with SHAP analysis independently confirming that CLC's contribution is positive in minority tracts and negative in white tracts. Taken all together, these findings provide the first tract-level evidence consistent with corporate landlord concentration being associated with disproportionately higher rent growth in communities of color.

title: Selling through Distributors in Developing Economies: Operations-Finance Coordination

detail.title: Selling through Distributors in Developing Economies: Operations-Finance Coordination
detail.abstract: Problem Definition: In developing economies, distributors often fulfill two roles when manufacturers sell to small retailers, such as nanostores, through them: boosting demand and providing financing. This paper examines how a manufacturer should contract with distributors to coordinate these two roles. Methodology and Results: We consider a game-theoretic model with a manufacturer who sells to nanostores through a distributor. The distributor both provides financing and helps boost retail demand. Financially constrained himself, the distributor may seek for bank financing. The distributor or the bank could also conduct due diligence to screen nanostores' capabilities, which affects retail demand and in turn the distributor's financial risk. We first examine a contract regime under which both the sales-boosting and due diligence efforts are delegated to the distributor ("bilateral contract"). Our analysis uncovers a tension between these two tasks. Consequently, under the optimal contract terms, the distributor exerts due diligence effort only when his working capital level is relatively high. This leaves markets with thin profit margins and high information acquisition costs underserved. To mitigate such inefficiencies, we propose a three-party contract where the manufacturer delegates due diligence, and hence credit granting, to the bank, while the distributor focuses on boosting sales ("trilateral contracting"). We find that such contracts can induce due diligence when the distributor's working capital is low, thus complementing the bilateral contracts. In addition to improving manufacturer profitability, the trilateral contract can expand the parameter regions for which the manufacturer is willing to serve the market. Managerial Implications: Our work provides a framework for manufacturers to design distributor contracts to better serve small retailers in emerging markets. We characterize how the choice of contract forms and terms is determined by various operational and financial conditions faced by the supply chain.

detail.abstract: This paper evaluates the effects of a conditional cash transfer (CCT) on antenatal consultations in Senegal. We conduct a non-experimental and a quasi-experimental evaluations, in which the control group is constructed using a propensity score matching method. While the non-experimental approach alone does not allow to conclude on the impact of the CCT, the quasi-experimental approach reveals that the CCT significatively increases antenatal consultations of beneficiaries. The combination of non-experimental and quasi-experimental evaluations has the potential to offer evaluation of social policies in a cost-effective way, using existing information, such as administrative data and already-collected survey data.

title: Eonism and the Aesthetic Unworking of Gender: Ontological Refusal, the Transvestite Sublime, and the Post-Transsexual Imagination from Ellis to Preciado - Eonism and the Transvestite Sublime: Aesthetic Identification as Ontological Refusal: From the Chevalier d'Éon to the Post-Transsexual Imagination

detail.title: Eonism and the Aesthetic Unworking of Gender: Ontological Refusal, the Transvestite Sublime, and the Post-Transsexual Imagination from Ellis to Preciado - Eonism and the Transvestite Sublime: Aesthetic Identification as Ontological Refusal: From the Chevalier d'Éon to the Post-Transsexual Imagination
detail.abstract: Havelock Ellis, in the seventh volume of his Studies in the Psychology of Sex (1928), bequeathed to the twentieth century a term at once exquisitely literary and stubbornly unassimilable by the clinical machinery that would follow: Eonism. Named for the Chevalier d’Éon—that uncanny eighteenth-century diplomat, spy, and transvestite who navigated the courts of Europe in a sustained state of gendered undecidability—the neologism designated a “sexo-aesthetic inversion” in which the subject does not merely desire the opposite sex but ontologically identifies with its aesthetic totality, “carrying that identification too far” until the imagination itself becomes the substance of the self (Ellis, 1928, p. 24). Ellis’s formulation, however biologized its underpinnings, opens a philosophical abyss: the Eonist is a being for whom the aesthetic attitude—ordinarily the contemplation of beauty at a distance—invades the very architecture of existence, transforming the donning of silk and lace from a sartorial act into an ontological relocation. The Eonist does not perform femininity; he becomes it, but through a becoming that is neither surgical nor hormonal, a becoming that unfolds entirely within the regime of the aesthetic. This essay traces the subterranean philosophical life of Eonism across a century of sexological, psychoanalytic, and queer-theoretical contestation, arguing that the concept constitutes a permanent crisis for any attempt to stabilize the categories of sexed being. By following the term’s entanglement with the transvestite, the transsexual, and the transgender, and by recovering the aesthetic dimension that each successive paradigm has suppressed, I propose that Eonism names nothing less than the aesthetic unworking of gender itself—an unworking that finds its most radical articulation in the post-transsexual imagination of Paul B. Preciado, where the body becomes a laboratory for the infinite plastic reinvention of the self.

title: The Adaptive Automotive Supplier: Integrating Governance Theories and Contemporary Risk Profiles

detail.title: The Adaptive Automotive Supplier: Integrating Governance Theories and Contemporary Risk Profiles

detail.abstract: Automotive suppliers are facing multiple, interconnected disruptions from vehicle electrification, software-defined vehicle architectures and a newly emergent phenomenon of geopolitical fragmentation and regionalization. This article integrates five pillars of management thinking (transaction cost economics, agency theory, game theory, global value chain theory and platform ecosystem theory) into a coherent whole explaining how these pressures transform OEM's supplier governance for a total of 423 articles published from 2010 to 2026. The findings suggest that existing supplier management literature mostly focuses on supply chain and strategic risks, with other risk types (contractual risk, technological risk and financial risk) frequently accompanying and co-occurring with them and that there is a severe shortage of implementation specificity: instead of providing a specific set of organizational capabilities, studies mostly outline risks or potential coping strategies. The study frames supplier adaptation to global transformations as a compound governance problem and outlines a staged agenda, encompassing sensing and diagnosing existing risks, adopting a governance response and lastly developing their capabilities for ensuring strategic significance within the global automotive OEM network considering asymmetric bargaining power in the setting of persistent volatility.

title: Key Problems of Using Subsidies Coupled With Agricultural Production
affiliations: National Research Institute (PIB) - Institute of Agricultural and Food Economics - National Research Institute (IAFE-NRI) and National Research Institute - Institute of Agricultural and Food Economics - National Research Institute (IAFE-NRI)

detail.title: Key Problems of Using Subsidies Coupled With Agricultural Production
detail.abstract: Subsidies based on agricultural production are a common form of subsidies in many countries, both less developed (due to their economic difficulties in achieving a satisfactory level of food self-sufficiency) and highly developed. However, at the turn of the 20 th and 21 st centuries, this support was not so popular. it was only in the second decade that it began to be restored, which is sometimes referred to as recoupling. The COVID-19 pandemic and the ukrainian-Russian war are undoubtedly two important circumstances that have increased interest in these subsidies. Therefore, it is important to identify theoretical and socio-political justifications for using these subsidies and the problems related to preparing schemes for determining their unit rates. after conducting the analysis, it turned out that the microeconomic theory rather provides arguments against the wide use of agricultural production subsidies. The justifications for pursuing a policy which refers to the difficulties in particular sectors of agriculture are also unconvincing. The calculation of unit payment rates is a challenge due to the lack of a solid methodology and sufficiently reliable source data.

title: Environmental Antimicrobial Stewardship Among Nurses in Kazakhstan: A Mixed-Methods Study
affiliations: Nazarbayev University, Nazarbayev University, University of Bologna, Nazarbayev University, Nazarbayev University, Astana Medical University, World Health Organization (WHO) - WHO European Office for the Prevention and Control of Noncommunicable Diseases and Nazarbayev University

detail.title: Environmental Antimicrobial Stewardship Among Nurses in Kazakhstan: A Mixed-Methods Study

declarations.declarationOfInterest: All authors declare no competing interests

All participants provided informed consent prior to data collection, with guaranteed anonymity and the right to withdraw at any stage.

detail.abstract:
Background; Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) poses a critical environmental threat, yet institutional factors shaping frontline stewardship practices remain poorly understood. Nurses occupy a central role in pharmaceutical handling and waste disposal, but evidence on how healthcare systems enable or obstruct the translation of stewardship knowledge into compliant practice is sparse. We investigated whether environmental stewardship failures among frontline nurses in Kazakhstan primarily reflect knowledge deficits or institutional and professional barriers to behavioural translation.

Methods: We conducted a parallel convergent mixed-methods study combining a cross-sectional survey of 25,609 nurses across all 20 administrative regions of Kazakhstan with 52 semi-structured interviews in sfindix tertiary hospitals. Multivariable logistic and linear regression models assessed associations between antibiotic disposal training, stewardship knowledge, professional responsibility perceptions, and disposal behaviours. Qualitative thematic analysis explored institutional mechanisms underlying quantitative patterns.

Findings: Of 25,609 nurses, 61·9% reported receiving antibiotic disposal training. Awareness of recommended disposal methods (89·6%) and environmental disposal risks (87·6%) was high, yet substantial behavioural gaps persisted. Among nurses with correct disposal knowledge (n=21,064), trained nurses had lower odds of non-compliant behaviour (OR 0·511, 95% CI 0·466–0·560). Employer-integrated training showed the strongest association with compliance (OR 0·368, 95% CI 0·299–0·453), whereas government and NGO training were paradoxically associated with higher odds of non-compliance. Qualitative analysis identified a responsibility gap, professional role silos, fragmented disposal protocols, and reduced frontline visibility of pharmaceutical waste as key barriers.

Interpretation: Environmental stewardship failures among nurses reflect institutional barriers to behavioural translation, not knowledge deficits alone. Stewardship responsibilities must be explicitly integrated into nursing roles, reinforced through workplace accountability mechanisms, and embedded within routine clinical workflows. Nurses represent a critical and underutilised resource within One Health AMR containment strategies.

title: The Impact of Non-Invasive EEG-Based Brain-Computer Interfaces on Motor Cortex Plasticity During Adult Motor Learning

detail.title: The Impact of Non-Invasive EEG-Based Brain-Computer Interfaces on Motor Cortex Plasticity During Adult Motor Learning
detail.abstract: Brain plasticity in adulthood refers to the capability of reorganizing the network of neurons that make up the brain. Recent advances in technology have enabled Electroencephalogram-based (EEG-based) Brain Computer Interfaces (BCIs) to move away from passive communication aid systems to becoming a therapy that can influence the motor cortex plasticity of the brain. In this review, we aim to explore the effectiveness of EEG-based BCIs in inducing brain plasticity and learning. BCIs close the loop between neuronal intent and sensory feedback, employing Hebbian learning to facilitate strengthening synaptic connections. The purpose of this review is to analyze the importance of the role played by sensorimotor rhythms (mu band and beta band), the similarities between motor imagery and execution in the neurophysiological perspective, and the progression from a lab-based, fixed paradigm to natural motor decoding. Moreover, this paper critically assesses the effectiveness of using BCI as a treatment tool for stroke rehabilitation, along with the associated technical difficulties of achieving BCI literacy and a high signal-to-noise ratio.

title: Looksmaxxing Men, Looksminimizing Women: Self-Improvement, Self-Aggrandizement, and the Aesthetics of the New Social Darwinism: A Critical Cultural Essay on Gender, Desire, the Pill Imaginary, and the Ghost of Körperkultur

detail.title: Looksmaxxing Men, Looksminimizing Women: Self-Improvement, Self-Aggrandizement, and the Aesthetics of the New Social Darwinism: A Critical Cultural Essay on Gender, Desire, the Pill Imaginary, and the Ghost of Körperkultur
detail.abstract:
Something strange is happening to the bodies of the digital age, and it is not merely cosmetic. In the subcultural trenches of forums, subreddits, TikTok feeds, and the labyrinthine underworld of the manosphere, a peculiar asymmetry has crystallized: men are instructed to maximize — to optimize, sculpt, and biohack their way toward an idealized masculine form — while women, at least those who perform legibility within the dominant liberal-progressive register, are increasingly instructed to minimize — to flatten, desexualize, and deaestheticize themselves under the banner of liberation from the male gaze. This asymmetry, which we might call the dialectic of looksmaxxing and looksminimizing, is not simply an accident of cultural drift, nor the innocent by-product of two parallel self-help movements. It is a structurally determined phenomenon arising from the intersection of neoliberal subjectification, the crisis of hegemonic masculinity, the commodification of intimacy, and the spectacular society’s terminal confusion between image and reality. It is, in the most precise sense, political — and it demands analysis that takes it seriously as such.

The concept of looksmaxxing — derived from the internet-subcultural fusion of “looks” and “maximizing” — refers to a broad and internally differentiated set of practices through which predominantly male users of incel-adjacent and manosphere communities seek to enhance their physical appearance, typically in order to ascend the hierarchical “sexual market value” (SMV) ranking that structures their social imaginary (Sousbois, 2025). These practices range from the relatively mundane — skincare, grooming, exercise — to the extreme and medically dubious: anabolic steroid regimens, invasive cosmetic surgery, manipulation of jaw musculature, and even the use of artificial intelligence to rate facial geometry against idealized “Chad” archetypes (Solea & Sugiura, 2025). What is philosophically interesting about looksmaxxing is not its content, which is often banal or pathetically self-defeating, but its structure: it represents a hypertrophied and ideologically saturated version of the classical concept of Bildung — self-cultivation and self-formation — deprived of any humanistic or ethical content and reduced to the raw arithmetic of visual value. Where Hegel understood Bildung as the process by which the subject comes to recognize itself in the Absolute through culture, history, and dialectical struggle, the looksmaxxer understands Bildung as the process by which the jawline comes to approximate the 1.618 ratio of the golden mean (Hegel, 1807/1977).

title: Barriers to a European Banking Union
affiliations: , International Monetary Fund (IMF),  and European Central Bank (ECB)

detail.title: Barriers to a European Banking Union

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We quantify barriers to cross-border banking within the euro area and their consequences for credit allocation and output. Using loan-level data from the European credit registry (AnaCredit) and group structures (RIAD), we estimate barriers to relationship formation, loan pricing, and banks’ branching decisions at the country-pair level. We find that barriers to cross-border relationships between banks and firms and cross-border bank entry are large while wedges on interest rates and loan quantities are comparatively small. The estimated edges are strongly associated with differences in national banking regulations, measured using a novel dataset on regulatory distances. We embed our estimates into a quantitative spatial general equilibrium model with heterogeneous banks and firms subject to cross-border frictions in relationship formation, loan pricing, and bank entry. Partially relaxing frictions predicts sizable and heterogeneous output gains across euro area countries. These gains are primarily driven by increases in capital and labor rather than improvements in allocative efficiency.

title: Drivers of Germany’s Growth Downturn
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Drivers of Germany’s Growth Downturn

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Germany’s economy experienced a pronounced recession during 2023–24, with real GDP contracting and growth falling notably behind the rest of the euro area. This paper systematically examines the underlying causes of this downturn using four complementary approaches. We find that about 60 percent of Germany’s growth underperformance was due to lower potential growth while about 40 percent reflected cyclical factors. The downturn was broad-based, with nearly all major expenditure categories—but particularly investment and exports—weighing on activity. On the production side, the recession was concentrated in manufacturing and construction, which together accounted for the bulk of the growth gap relative to the euro area. The analysis further shows that the decline in output was driven primarily by falling productivity, especially in industry and construction, rather than by a reduction in hours worked. This decline in productivity partly reflected cyclical labor hoarding amid weak aggregate demand. However, structural challenges—including (i) longer-term subdued productivity growth due to structural factors such as persistent underinvestment in public infrastructure, skills, and innovation as well as excessive red tape; (ii) population aging; (iii) one-off adverse effects from the 2022 energy-price shock, and (iv) deteriorating external competitiveness (although the level of the current account surplus remains substantial)—amplified the cyclical downturn.

title: The EU’s Recovery and Resilience Facility
affiliations: , International Monetary Fund (IMF) and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: The EU’s Recovery and Resilience Facility

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper takes stock of the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF)’s economic impact as implementation enters its final phase and draws lessons for the design of the next EU Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF). Using sectoral and cross-country data, the paper finds that the RRF provided a short term demand boost, supporting employment and output growth—especially in countries with large allocations—while a substantial share of its growth impact is expected to materialize as absorption accelerates. Unprecedented joint EU level borrowing is found to have contributed to stabilizing sovereign debt markets and improving prospects for EU bonds as safe assets. Finally, the RRF’s performance based conditionality through improved national ownership has supported reform implementation in some member states. At the same time, challenges around the pace of funds absorption remain as implementation is still ramping up and the overall macroeconomic impact will ultimately depend on how effectively the RRF funds are utilized. Plan overambition and complexity, administrative capacity limits, and absorption bottlenecks have slowed disbursement in several member states, while the predominance of output based milestones and targets has limited the framework’s focus on results.

title: Persistent Temperature, Capital Structure, and the Long-Run Level of Output
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Persistent Temperature, Capital Structure, and the Long-Run Level of Output

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper shows that separating persistent (permanent) temperature changes from transitory weather fluctuations can reshape our understanding of the macroeconomic costs of warming. Using a Kalman filter state-space decomposition, it separates temperature into a permanent component and transitory weather fluctuations, and links the permanent component to trend output using a panel cointegration and error-correction framework. A one-degree Celsius higher permanent temperature is associated with a significant decline in the long-run level of output, with full adjustment unfolding over multiple decades to a century. Decomposing aggregate output into population and output per capita reveals that the long-run output losses operate primarily through demographic adjustment in the full sample, while in advanced economies, both long-run output per capita and population decline as the climate warms. Economies with higher capital intensity and more durable capital stocks experience larger long-run per capita output losses. These findings suggest that long-run economic vulnerability to persistent warming is more broadly distributed across rich and poor countries than the short-run weather literature implies, reflecting differences in capital structure. They complement rather than contradict the well-established finding that developing countries are more exposed to short-run weather shocks.

title: The Growth Effects of Natural Disasters
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF) - Fiscal Affairs Department,  and

detail.title: The Growth Effects of Natural Disasters

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We construct standardized climate anomalies from daily observations and carefully calibrate physical thresholds to identify storms, floods, droughts, heatwaves, and cold snaps across 196 countries over the period 1970–2023. Using a local projections framework, we estimate the contemporaneous and 2-year effects of each disaster type and collectively on real GDP growth. We find that storms, floods, droughts, and heatwaves significantly reduce growth on impact (by roughly 0.1–0.2 percentage points on average), with the largest effects observed in emerging markets and developing economies. Cold spells have no statistically significant impacts. Our estimations also indicate that the initial drop in GDP growth is often not fully offset by a quick rebound, leaving GDP below the pre-disaster trend in the subsequent two years. Severe disasters impose far larger costs. Catastrophic floods can lower growth by up to 3 percentage points (with once-in-100-year storms or heatwaves reducing growth by ~0.5pp and extreme droughts by ~1pp). By combining the estimated global coefficients with each country’s own disaster intensity, we translate the aggregate results into localized growth effects and cross-check them against estimates from a dynamic heterogenous panel model. Finally, rolling-window estimates indicate that the contemporaneous growth impact of storms and heatwaves has attenuated in recent decades, whereas droughts have become increasingly damaging, reflecting divergent adaptation or even maladaptation and vulnerability trends over time.

title: Targeting State Aid
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF) and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Targeting State Aid

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper examines the firm-level impact of state aid in France from 2016–23 and how targeting affects economic outcomes. Using firm-level data and a difference-in-differences approach, we find that aid is most effective for young firms, improving real outcomes while also crowding in private debt financing. Size-based targeting, by contrast, has limited impact. R&D support is particularly effective for young firms in high-tech sectors, and energy aid has the strongest effects in manufacturing, pointing to its potential role in helping firms reduce emissions and facilitating the green transition.
